The provided text details several methods and options for managing browser and API request contexts in Playwright:

**BrowserContext Management**
*   **Cookies:** 
    *   `addCookies`: Adds cookies to a browser context, which are then installed across all pages within that context. It requires an array of cookie objects. For each cookie, either a `url` or both a `domain` and `path` must be provided, along with a `name` and `value`.
    *   `cookies()`: A method used to obtain cookies.
*   **Storage State:**
    *   `storageState()`: Captures a snapshot of the storage state. It can take an optional `options` object where `path` specifies the file to save the state to (relative paths are resolved to the current working directory). If no path is provided, the state is returned but not saved to disk. An `indexedDB` boolean option (added in v1.51) allows the inclusion of IndexedDB, which is useful for applications like Firebase Authentication.
    *   `setStorageState()`: Applies a storage state to the context, accepting either a file path (string) or a storage state object containing an array of cookies (where `domain` and `path` are required).
*   **HTTP Credentials:**
    *   `setHTTPCredentials()`: Sets the `username` and `password` for the context.

**APIRequestContext Management**
*   **Storage State:** Similar to the browser context, if a `path` is provided for the storage state, relative paths are resolved to the current working directory. If no path is provided, the storage state is returned without being saved to disk. The returned object includes an array of `cookies` containing `name` and `value` strings.

###### ​ {#-6}

### Preserve authenticated state​ {#preserve-authenticated-state}

Run
`codegen`
with
`--save-storage`
to save
cookies (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Cookies)
,
localStorage (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage)
and
IndexedDB (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IndexedDB_API)
data at the end of the session. This is useful to separately record an authentication step and reuse it later when recording more tests.


`npx playwright codegen github.com/microsoft/playwright --save-storage=auth.json`


###### ​ {#-7}

#### Login​ {#login}

After performing authentication and closing the browser,
`auth.json`
will contain the storage state which you can then reuse in your tests.

Make sure you only use the
`auth.json`
locally as it contains sensitive information. Add it to your
`.gitignore`
or delete it once you have finished generating your tests.

#### Load authenticated state​ {#load-authenticated-state}

Run with
`--load-storage`
to consume the previously loaded storage from the
`auth.json`
. This way, all
cookies (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Cookies)
,
localStorage (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage)
and
IndexedDB (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IndexedDB_API)
data will be restored, bringing most web apps to the authenticated state without the need to login again. This means you can continue generating tests from the logged in state.


`npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json github.com/microsoft/playwright`


###### ​ {#-8}

#### Use existing userDataDir​ {#use-existing-userdatadir}

Run
`codegen`
with
`--user-data-dir`
to set a fixed
user data directory (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-launch-persistent-context-option-user-data-dir)
for the browser session. If you create a custom browser user data directory, codegen will use this existing browser profile and have access to any authentication state present in that profile.

As of Chrome 136, the default user data directory cannot be accessed via automated tooling (https://developer.chrome.com/blog/remote-debugging-port)
, such as Playwright. You must create a separate user data directory for use in testing.

## Record using custom setup​ {#record-using-custom-setup}

If you would like to use codegen in some non-standard setup (for example, use
browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route)
), it is possible to call

`const{chromium}=require('@playwright/test');(async()=>{// Make sure to run headed.constbrowser=awaitchromium.launch({headless:false});// Setup context however you like.constcontext=awaitbrowser.newContext({/* pass any options */});awaitcontext.route('**/*',route=>route.continue());// Pause the page, and start recording manually.constpage=awaitcontext.newPage();awaitpage.pause();})();`

The provided text details the methods available within the Playwright `BrowserContext` class:

**Cookie and Storage Management**
*   **`addCookies`**: Adds cookies to the browser context, which are then installed across all pages. Required fields are either a `url` or both `domain` and `path`.
*   **`clearCookies`**: Removes cookies from the context. It accepts an optional filter to target specific cookies by `domain`, `name`, or `path` (using strings or Regular Expressions).
*   **`cookies`**: Retrieves cookies from the context, with an optional argument to filter by a list of URLs.
*   **`storageState`**: Returns the current storage state, including cookies, local storage, and IndexedDB snapshots (the latter must be explicitly enabled via options). It can also save this state directly to a file path.
*   **`setStorageState`**: Populates the context with a given storage state (from a file or object), often used to initialize a context with logged-in information.

**Scripting and Bindings**
*   **`addInitScript`**: Adds a script to be evaluated whenever a page is created, navigated, or a child frame is attached/navigated. It runs after the document is created but before any other scripts execute.
*   **`exposeBinding`**: Adds a function to the `window` object of every frame in every page. When called, it executes a callback that receives information about the caller (browser context, page, and frame).

**Context Control and Permissions**
*   **`close`**: Closes the browser context and all associated pages. Note that the default browser context cannot be closed.
*   **`clearPermissions`**: Removes all permission overrides for the context.
*   **`browser`**: Returns the Browser object associated with the context, or null.

**Network Routing**
*   **`unroute`**: Removes routes previously created with `browserContext.route()`. It can remove all routes for a specific URL or a specific handler for a URL.

# Authentication | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/auth/>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this
`playwright/.auth`
directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.

danger
The browser state file may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account. We strongly discourage checking them into private or public repositories.

Bash
PowerShell
Batch

`mkdir-pplaywright/.authecho$'\nplaywright/.auth'>>.gitignore`


`New-Item-ItemType Directory-Force-Path playwright\.authAdd-Content-path.gitignore"`r`nplaywright/.auth"`


`mdplaywright\.authecho. >> .gitignoreecho"playwright/.auth">> .gitignore`


## Basic: shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

Details

Create
`tests/auth.setup.ts`
that will prepare authenticated browser state for all other tests.

tests/auth.setup.ts

`import{testassetup,expect}from'@playwright/test';importpathfrom'path';constauthFile=path.join(__dirname,'../playwright/.auth/user.json');setup('authenticate',async({page})=>{// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('username');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:authFile});});`


Create a new
`setup`
project in the config and declare it as a
dependency (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-projects#dependencies)
for all your testing projects. This project will always run and authenticate before all the tests. All testing projects should use the authenticated state as
`storageState`
.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig,devices}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({projects:[// Setup project{name:'setup',testMatch:/.*\.setup\.ts/},{name:'chromium',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome'],// Use prepared auth state.storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json',},dependencies:['setup'],},{name:'firefox',use:{...devices['Desktop Firefox'],// Use prepared auth state.storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json',},dependencies:['setup'],},],});`


Tests start already authenticated because we specified
`storageState`
in the config.

tests/example.spec.ts

`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test('test',async({page})=>{// page is authenticated});`

### Example​ {#example}

Here is a global setup example that authenticates once and reuses authentication state in tests. It uses the
`baseURL`
and
`storageState`
options from the configuration file.

global-setup.ts

`import{chromium,typeFullConfig}from'@playwright/test';asyncfunctionglobalSetup(config:FullConfig){const{baseURL,storageState}=config.projects[0].use;constbrowser=awaitchromium.launch();constpage=awaitbrowser.newPage();awaitpage.goto(baseURL!);awaitpage.getByLabel('User Name').fill('user');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByText('Sign in').click();awaitpage.context().storageState({path:storageStateasstring});awaitbrowser.close();}exportdefaultglobalSetup;`


Specify
`globalSetup`
,
`baseURL`
and
`storageState`
in the configuration file.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({globalSetup:require.resolve('./global-setup'),use:{baseURL:'http://localhost:3000/',storageState:'state.json',},});`


Tests start already authenticated because we specify
`storageState`
that was populated by global setup.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test('test',async({page})=>{awaitpage.goto('/');// You are signed in!});`


You can make arbitrary data available in your tests from your global setup file by setting them as environment variables via
`process.env`
.

global-setup.ts

`importtype{FullConfig}from'@playwright/test';asyncfunctionglobalSetup(config:FullConfig){process.env.FOO='some data';// Or a more complicated data structure as JSON:process.env.BAR=JSON.stringify({some:'data'});}exportdefaultglobalSetup;`


Tests have access to the
`process.env`
properties set in the global setup.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test('test',async({page})=>{// environment variables which are set in globalSetup are only available inside test().const{FOO,BAR}=process.env;// FOO and BAR properties are populated.expect(FOO).toEqual('some data');constcomplexData=JSON.parse(BAR);expect(BAR).toEqual({some:'data'});});`


### Capturing trace of failures during global setup​ {#capturing-trace-of-failures-during-global-setup}

In some instances, it may be useful to capture a trace of failures encountered during the global setup. In order to do this, you must
start tracing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-tracing#tracing-start)
in your setup, and you must ensure that you
stop tracing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-tracing#tracing-stop)
if an error occurs before that error is thrown. This can be achieved by wrapping your setup in a
`try...catch`
block.  Here is an example that expands the global setup example to capture a trace.

global-setup.ts

`import{chromium,typeFullConfig}from'@playwright/test';asyncfunctionglobalSetup(config:FullConfig){const{baseURL,storageState}=config.projects[0].use;constbrowser=awaitchromium.launch();constcontext=awaitbrowser.newContext();constpage=awaitcontext.newPage();try{awaitcontext.tracing.start({screenshots:true,snapshots:true});awaitpage.goto(baseURL!);awaitpage.getByLabel('User Name').fill('user');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByText('Sign in').click();awaitcontext.storageState({path:storageStateasstring});awaitcontext.tracing.stop({path:'./test-results/setup-trace.zip',});awaitbrowser.close();}catch(error){awaitcontext.tracing.stop({path:'./test-results/failed-setup-trace.zip',});awaitbrowser.close();throwerror;}}exportdefaultglobalSetup;`

### Multiple signed in roles​ {#multiple-signed-in-roles}

When to use

You have more than one role in your end to end tests, but you can reuse accounts across all tests.

Details

We will authenticate multiple times in the setup project.

tests/auth.setup.ts

`import{testassetup,expect}from'@playwright/test';constadminFile='playwright/.auth/admin.json';setup('authenticate as admin',async({page})=>{// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('admin');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:adminFile});});constuserFile='playwright/.auth/user.json';setup('authenticate as user',async({page})=>{// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('user');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:userFile});});`


After that, specify
`storageState`
for each test file or test group,
instead of
setting it in the config.

tests/example.spec.ts

`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.use({storageState:'playwright/.auth/admin.json'});test('admin test',async({page})=>{// page is authenticated as admin});test.describe(()=>{test.use({storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json'});test('user test',async({page})=>{// page is authenticated as a user});});`


See also about
authenticating in the UI mode (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/auth/#authenticating-in-ui-mode)
.

### Testing multiple roles together​ {#testing-multiple-roles-together}

When to use

You need to test how multiple authenticated roles interact together, in a single test.

Details

Use multiple
BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext)
s and
Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page)
s with different storage states in the same test.

tests/example.spec.ts

`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test('admin and user',async({browser})=>{// adminContext and all pages inside, including adminPage, are signed in as "admin".constadminContext=awaitbrowser.newContext({storageState:'playwright/.auth/admin.json'});constadminPage=awaitadminContext.newPage();// userContext and all pages inside, including userPage, are signed in as "user".constuserContext=awaitbrowser.newContext({storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json'});constuserPage=awaituserContext.newPage();// ... interact with both adminPage and userPage ...awaitadminContext.close();awaituserContext.close();});`

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test includes the ability to produce and visually compare screenshots using
`await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()`
. On first execution, Playwright test will generate reference screenshots. Subsequent runs will compare against the reference.

example.spec.ts

`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('example test',async({page})=>{awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev');awaitexpect(page).toHaveScreenshot();});`


warning
Browser rendering can vary based on the host OS, version, settings, hardware, power source (battery vs. power adapter), headless mode, and other factors. For consistent screenshots, run tests in the same environment where the baseline screenshots were generated.

## Generating screenshots​ {#generating-screenshots}

When you run above for the first time, test runner will say:


`Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.`


That's because there was no golden file yet. This method took a bunch of screenshots until two consecutive screenshots matched, and saved the last screenshot to file system. It is now ready to be added to the repository.

The name of the folder with the golden expectations starts with the name of your test file:


`drwxr-xr-x5user  group160Jun411:46.drwxr-xr-x6user  group192Jun411:45..-rw-r--r--1user  group231Jun411:16 example.spec.tsdrwxr-xr-x3user  group96Jun411:46 example.spec.ts-snapshots`


The snapshot name
`example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png`
consists of a few parts:

`example-test-1.png`
- an auto-generated name of the snapshot. Alternatively you can specify snapshot name as the first argument of the
`toHaveScreenshot()`
method:

`awaitexpect(page).toHaveScreenshot('landing.png');`

`chromium-darwin`
- the browser name and the platform. Screenshots differ between browsers and platforms due to different rendering, fonts and more, so you will need different snapshots for them. If you use multiple projects in your
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
, project name will be used instead of
`chromium`
.

The snapshot name and path can be configured with
testConfig.snapshotPathTemplate (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-snapshot-path-template)
in the playwright config.

Note that
`toHaveScreenshot()`
also accepts an array of path segments to the snapshot file such as
`expect().toHaveScreenshot(['relative', 'path', 'to', 'snapshot.png'])`
.
However, this path must stay within the snapshots directory for each test file (i.e.
`a.spec.js-snapshots`
), otherwise it will throw.

To pin the browser to a specific GPS location for a test, you can use the following methods:

*   **In the configuration file (`playwright.config.ts`):** Set the `geolocation` property within the `use` object, providing the `longitude` and `latitude`. You should also include `'geolocation'` in the `permissions` array.
*   **Using `browser.newContext`:** Pass a `geolocation` object containing the `longitude` and `latitude`, and include `'geolocation'` in the `permissions` array.
*   **Changing the location during a test:** Use the `browserContext.setGeolocation` method with an object containing the `longitude` and `latitude`.

**Geolocation Object Properties:**
*   **latitude**: A number between -90 and 90.
*   **longitude**: A number between -180 and 180.
*   **accuracy**: An optional non-negative number (defaults to 0).

It is recommended to use `browserContext.grantPermissions()` to ensure pages within the browser context have the necessary permissions to read the geolocation.

The provided text details the configuration and management of geolocation and offline status within a browser environment.

**Geolocation Configuration**
Geolocation can be set using an object containing the following properties:
*   **latitude**: A number between -90 and 90.
*   **longitude**: A number between -180 and 180.
*   **accuracy**: An optional non-negative number that defaults to 0.

Depending on the method used, passing `null` has different effects:
*   In certain browser options, passing `null` resets emulation to system defaults (with a default of `'none'`).
*   When using `browserContext.setGeolocation`, passing `null` or `undefined` emulates a position that is unavailable.

For `browserContext.setGeolocation`, it is recommended to use `browserContext.grantPermissions()` to ensure pages within the browser context have permission to read the geolocation. This method returns a `Promise<void>`.

**Other Browser Context Settings**
*   **setOffline**: The `browserContext.setOffline` method allows for setting the offline status.

The provided text outlines various options for launching a browser on an Android device:

*   **Geolocation**: An optional object that allows setting the `latitude` (between -90 and 90) and `longitude` (between -180 and 180). It also includes an optional `accuracy` value, which is non-negative and defaults to `0`. Passing `null` resets emulation to system defaults, while the default setting is `'none'`.
*   **Locale**: An optional string (e.g., `en-GB`, `de-DE`) used to specify the user locale. This affects the `Accept-Language` request header, `navigator.language` value, and date and number formatting. It defaults to the system default locale.
*   **Timezone**: The `timezoneId` is an optional string that changes the context's timezone based on ICU's metaZones.txt. It defaults to the system timezone.
*   **Viewport**: An optional object or `null` used to emulate a consistent viewport for each page. It requires `width` and `height` in pixels and defaults to 1280x720.
*   **User Agent**: An optional string used to specify a specific user agent for the context.
*   **JavaScript**: Defaults to `true`.
*   **Strict Selectors Mode**: Defaults to `false`. In this mode, operations on selectors implying a single target DOM element will throw an error if more than one element matches. This does not affect Locator APIs.
*   **Logger**: An optional Logger that is now deprecated because the logs it receives are incomplete; tracing is recommended instead.

To interact with a button rendered inside an iframe, you can use the `page.frameLocator()` method. This creates a frame locator that enters the iframe and allows you to select elements within it.

`const locator = page.frameLocator('#my-iframe').getByText('Submit');`

The provided text details the methods available for the `ElementHandle` and `Frame` classes in Playwright.

### ElementHandle Methods
*   **boundingBox**: Returns the element's bounding box (x, y, width, height) relative to the main frame viewport. It returns `null` if the element is not visible.
*   **contentFrame**: Returns the content frame for handles referencing iframe nodes, otherwise returns `null`.
*   **ownerFrame**: Returns the frame that contains the given element.
*   **scrollIntoViewIfNeeded**: Scrolls the element into view after performing actionability checks, unless it is already completely visible.
*   **selectOption**: Selects options in a `<select>` element (or an associated control of a `<label>`). It triggers `change` and `input` events and returns the selected option values.
*   **uncheck**: Ensures an element is a checkbox or radio input and unchecks it. It performs actionability checks, scrolls the element into view, and clicks the center of the element.
*   **waitForSelector**: Waits for a selector relative to the element handle to satisfy a specific state (appear/disappear from DOM or become visible/hidden).

### Frame Methods
*   **click**: Finds an element by selector and clicks its center (or a specified position) after actionability checks and scrolling.
*   **dblclick**: Performs a double click on an element matching a selector, dispatching two `click` events and one `dblclick` event.
*   **dispatchEvent**: Dispatches a specified event type (e.g., 'click') on an element, regardless of visibility.
*   **uncheck**: Similar to the `ElementHandle` version, it unchecks a checkbox or radio input matching a selector.
*   **waitForNavigation**: (Deprecated) Waits for frame navigation and returns the main resource response. Users are encouraged to use `frame.waitForURL()` instead.
*   **waitForSelector**: Waits for a selector to satisfy a state (`attached`, `detached`, `visible`, or `hidden`). It returns an `ElementHandle` or `null`.
*   **waitForTimeout**: (Discouraged) Waits for a specified number of milliseconds; intended for debugging rather than production tests.

The
locator.press() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-press)
method focuses the selected element and produces a single keystroke. It accepts the logical key names that are emitted in the
keyboardEvent.key (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/KeyboardEvent/key)
property of the keyboard events:


`Backquote, Minus, Equal, Backslash, Backspace, Tab, Delete, Escape,ArrowDown, End, Enter, Home, Insert, PageDown, PageUp, ArrowRight,ArrowUp, F1 - F12, Digit0 - Digit9, KeyA - KeyZ, etc.`


You can alternatively specify a single character you'd like to produce such as
`"a"`
or
`"#"`
.
Following modification shortcuts are also supported:
`Shift, Control, Alt, Meta`
.

Simple version produces a single character. This character is case-sensitive, so
`"a"`
and
`"A"`
will produce different results.


`// <input id=name>awaitpage.locator('#name').press('Shift+A');// <input id=name>awaitpage.locator('#name').press('Shift+ArrowLeft');`


Shortcuts such as
`"Control+o"`
or
`"Control+Shift+T"`
are supported as well. When specified with the modifier, modifier is pressed and being held while the subsequent key is being pressed.

Note that you still need to specify the capital
`A`
in
`Shift-A`
to produce the capital character.
`Shift-a`
produces a lower-case one as if you had the
`CapsLock`
toggled.

# Projects | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-projects/>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

A project is logical group of tests running with the same configuration. We use projects so we can run tests on different browsers and devices. Projects are configured in the
`playwright.config.ts`
file and once configured you can then run your tests on all projects or only on a specific project. You can also use projects to run the same tests in different configurations. For example, you can run the same tests in a logged-in and logged-out state.

By setting up projects you can also run a group of tests with different timeouts or retries or a group of tests against different environments such as staging and production, splitting tests per package/functionality and more.

## Configure projects for multiple browsers​ {#configure-projects-for-multiple-browsers}

By using
projects
you can run your tests in multiple browsers such as chromium, webkit and firefox as well as branded browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. Playwright can also run on emulated tablet and mobile devices. See the
registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json)
for a complete list of selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices.


`import{defineConfig,devices}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({projects:[{name:'chromium',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome']},},{name:'firefox',use:{...devices['Desktop Firefox']},},{name:'webkit',use:{...devices['Desktop Safari']},},/* Test against mobile viewports. */{name:'Mobile Chrome',use:{...devices['Pixel 5']},},{name:'Mobile Safari',use:{...devices['iPhone 12']},},/* Test against branded browsers. */{name:'Microsoft Edge',use:{...devices['Desktop Edge'],channel:'msedge'},},{name:'Google Chrome',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome'],channel:'chrome'},},],});`


## Run projects​ {#run-projects}

Playwright will run all projects by default.


`npx playwrighttestRunning7tests using5workers✓[chromium]› example.spec.ts:3:1 › basictest(2s)✓[firefox]› example.spec.ts:3:1 › basictest(2s)✓[webkit]› example.spec.ts:3:1 › basictest(2s)✓[Mobile Chrome]› example.spec.ts:3:1 › basictest(2s)✓[Mobile Safari]› example.spec.ts:3:1 › basictest(2s)✓[Microsoft Edge]› example.spec.ts:3:1 › basictest(2s)✓[Google Chrome]› example.spec.ts:3:1 › basictest(2s)`


Use the
`--project`
command line option to run a single project.


`npx playwrighttest--project=firefoxRunning1testusing1worker✓[firefox]› example.spec.ts:3:1 › basictest(2s)`


The VS Code test runner runs your tests on the default browser of Chrome. To run on other/multiple browsers click the play button's dropdown from the testing sidebar and choose another profile or modify the default profile by clicking
Select Default Profile
and select the browsers you wish to run your tests on.

Choose a specific profile, various profiles or all profiles to run tests on.

## Configure projects for multiple environments​ {#configure-projects-for-multiple-environments}

By setting up projects we can also run a group of tests with different timeouts or retries or run a group of tests against different environments. For example we can run our tests against a staging environment with 2 retries as well as against a production environment with 0 retries.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({timeout:60000,// Timeout is shared between all tests.projects:[{name:'staging',use:{baseURL:'staging.example.com',},retries:2,},{name:'production',use:{baseURL:'production.example.com',},retries:0,},],});`

For example, you can create a login test that runs first, then reuse that authenticated state across multiple tests without having to log in again for each test. In VS Code, you can see these setup tests in the Test Explorer and run them independently when needed.

To learn more, see our
Project Dependencies guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-projects)
.

### Global Setup​ {#global-setup}

For tasks that need to run only once before all tests (like seeding a database), use
Global Setup
. You can trigger the global setup and teardown manually from the Playwright sidebar.

### Multiple Configurations​ {#multiple-configurations}

If you have multiple
`playwright.config.ts`
files, you can switch between them using the gear icon in the Playwright sidebar. This allows you to easily work with different test suites or environments.

# Parallelism | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-parallel/>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-parallel/#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure
entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable
parallelism limit the number of
workers to one (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-parallel/#disable-parallelism)
.

You can control the number of
parallel worker processes (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-parallel/#limit-workers)
and
limit the number of failures (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-parallel/#limit-failures-and-fail-fast)
in the whole test suite for efficiency.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

## Limit workers​ {#limit-workers}

You can control the maximum number of parallel worker processes via
command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli)
or in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

From the command line:


`npx playwrighttest--workers4`


In the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Limit the number of workers on CI, use default locallyworkers:process.env.CI?2:undefined,});`


## Disable parallelism​ {#disable-parallelism}

You can disable any parallelism by allowing just a single worker at any time. Either set
`workers: 1`
option in the configuration file or pass
`--workers=1`
to the command line.


`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`


## Parallelize tests in a single file​ {#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file}

By default, tests in a single file are run in order. If you have many independent tests in a single file, you might want to run them in parallel with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.

Note that parallel tests are executed in separate worker processes and cannot share any state or global variables. Each test executes all relevant hooks just for itself, including
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'parallel'});test('runs in parallel 1',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('runs in parallel 2',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


Alternatively, you can opt-in all tests into this fully-parallel mode in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({fullyParallel:true,});`


You can also opt in for fully-parallel mode for just a few projects:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// runs all tests in all files of a specific project in parallelprojects:[{name:'chromium',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome']},fullyParallel:true,},]});`

Playwright is a testing framework offering tools for environment management, configuration, and test execution.

**Test Execution and Control**
Tests are run using `npx playwright test`. Execution can be filtered by tags, titles, line numbers, or file paths using `--grep` and `--grep-invert`. Available modes include headed, debug, and interactive UI. While files run in parallel by default using OS worker processes, tests within a file run sequentially unless configured otherwise via `fullyParallel: true` or `test.describe.configure({mode: 'parallel'})`. Inter-dependent tests can use `serial` mode, and large suites can be distributed across machines using `--shard`. Resource control is managed via `--workers` for parallelization and `--max-failures` to stop execution after a set number of failures.

**Configuration and Setup**
Settings are managed in `playwright.config.ts` via `defineConfig`, with options for `testDir`, `outputDir`, `retries`, `webServer`, and a default `timeout` of 30 seconds. Global lifecycle events are handled through `globalSetup`/`globalTeardown` or Project Dependencies. Browser dependencies are managed with `npx playwright install`, and caches are cleared using `npx playwright clear-cache`.

**Assertions and Annotations**
The `expect` function is used for assertions:
*   **Auto-retrying:** Web-specific matchers (e.g., `toBeVisible()`) retry for up to 5 seconds.
*   **Non-retrying:** Generic matchers like `toBe()` and `toEqual()`.
*   **Advanced:** Includes `expect.soft()`, `expect.poll`, `expect.toPass`, custom error messages, and `expect.extend` for custom matchers.
Tests can be annotated with `test.skip()`, `test.fail()`, `test.fixme()`, `test.only()`, or `test.slow()` (which triples the timeout).

**Fixtures**
Fixtures provide isolated environments. Built-in options include `page`, `context`, `browser`, `browserName`, and `request`. Custom fixtures are created via `test.extend()` and can be worker-scoped, test-scoped, automatic, or declarative options.

**Specialized Tools and Component Testing**
CLI tools include `codegen` for recording tests, `show-report` and `show-trace` for analysis, and `merge-reports` for combining blob reports. Experimental component testing for React and Vue allows components to run in real browsers using a `mount` fixture (with `update` and `unmount` methods), `beforeMount`/`afterMount` hooks, and an experimental `router` fixture for network interception.

The provided text outlines the configuration, execution, and parallelism features of Playwright Test.

### **Configuration**
Playwright allows test configuration via a configuration file using `defineConfig`. Key options include:
*   **Test Execution:** `testDir` specifies the test directory, `fullyParallel` enables parallel execution across all files, and `retries` sets the maximum retry attempts per test.
*   **CI/CD Integration:** `forbidOnly` can fail builds if `test.only` is left in the code, and `workers` can be adjusted based on the environment (e.g., limiting workers on CI).
*   **Environment & Infrastructure:** `webServer` can launch a local server before tests, and `projects` allow running tests across multiple browser configurations.
*   **Filtering:** Tests can be filtered using `testMatch` and `testIgnore` with glob patterns or regular expressions.

### **Parallelism and Worker Processes**
Playwright runs tests in parallel using independent OS worker processes.
*   **Execution Logic:** By default, test files run in parallel, but tests within a single file run sequentially. Parallelism within a single file can be enabled via `test.describe.configure({mode: 'parallel'})` or the `fullyParallel` config option.
*   **Worker Management:** Parallelism can be disabled by setting `workers: 1`. The number of failures can be limited using `maxFailures` to save resources.
*   **Worker Identification:** Each worker has a `workerIndex` (unique) and a `parallelIndex`. These can be used to isolate test data (e.g., creating unique database users per worker).
*   **Test Order:** When parallelism is disabled, tests run in alphabetical order by filename or via a "test list" file.

### **Fixtures**
Fixtures provide a way to set up and tear down environments for tests.
*   **Execution Order:** Setup runs before the test/hook, and teardown runs after. Fixtures follow dependency rules (dependency B is set up before A and torn down after A).
*   **Scopes:** Test-scoped fixtures are torn down after each test; worker-scoped fixtures are torn down only when the worker process ends.
*   **Types:** Automatic fixtures run regardless of whether they are explicitly called, while non-automatic fixtures are executed lazily.
*   **Customization:** Fixtures can be merged from multiple modules using `mergeTests`, given custom titles for reports, or "boxed" (`box: true`) to hide them from UI reports and traces.

### **Global Setup and Teardown**
There are two primary methods for global configuration:
1.  **Project Dependencies (Recommended):** Defining a setup project that runs before others. This method is preferred because it supports Playwright fixtures, trace recording, and is visible in HTML reports.
2.  **`globalSetup` Config Option:** A separate setup file that is more manual and does not support fixtures or trace recording.

Playwright Test offers a comprehensive suite of features for configuration, execution, and debugging:

**Test Configuration and Execution**
*   **Projects:** Tests can be organized into projects to run across different browsers (Chromium, WebKit, Firefox), branded browsers, or emulated devices. Projects can be used to parametrize tests, target different environments (staging vs. production), or manage different states (logged-in vs. logged-out). Projects can have dependencies (e.g., a "setup" project) and associated teardown processes.
*   **Execution Modes:** Tests run in independent worker processes. While isolated Pages are standard, `test.describe.serial()` allows for dependent tests to run in order and share a single Page.
*   **Retries and Filtering:** Failing tests can be retried globally, via command line, or for specific groups, resulting in "passed," "flaky," or "failed" categorizations. Tests can be filtered using `--grep`, `--shard`, or `--project`.
*   **Timeout Management:** Playwright utilizes multiple timeout levels, including a default 30s test timeout, a 5s expect timeout for auto-retrying assertions, a global timeout for the entire run, and specific timeouts for hooks, fixtures, actions, and navigation.

**Scaling and Reporting**
*   **Sharding:** To reduce runtime, tests can be split into shards using `--shard=x/y`. Distribution is handled at the test level if `fullyParallel` is true, otherwise it is handled at the file level.
*   **Reporters:** 
    *   **Built-in:** Options include List, Line, Dot (CI default), HTML, and GitHub Actions.
    *   **Blob Reporter:** Specifically designed for sharding; it saves results as `.zip` files that can be merged into a single report using `npx playwright merge-reports`.
    *   **JSON and JUnit:** Produce structured data/XML reports with configurable output names.
    *   **Custom:** Users can implement the `Reporter` API to create custom reporting classes.

**Parameterization and Visual Testing**
*   **Parameterization:** Tests can be dynamically generated using `forEach` loops, project-level overrides in the config file, environment variables (`process.env`), or by parsing CSV files.
*   **Visual Comparisons:** Playwright supports visual regression testing via `toHaveScreenshot()`, which compares current results against "golden" reference images. These can be updated with `--update-snapshots` and customized using `maxDiffPixels` or `stylePath`. Text or binary data can be compared using `toMatchSnapshot()`.

**UI Mode**
Launched via `npx playwright test --ui`, this interactive environment provides:
*   **Test Management:** A sidebar for filtering and running specific tests or projects.
*   **Debugging:** A time-travel timeline to view "Before" and "After" DOM snapshots, a "Pick locator" tool, and detailed tabs for network requests, console logs, and metadata.
*   **Additional Tools:** Watch mode for automatic re-runs, image comparison sliders for snapshots, and support for remote environments like Docker.

Playwright is a testing framework that provides comprehensive tools for test execution, configuration, and environment management.

### Test Execution and Control
Tests are executed via `npx playwright test` with several filtering and control options:
*   **Filtering:** Users can target specific tests using file paths, line numbers, titles, or tags via the `--grep` (or `-g`) and `--grep-invert` flags.
*   **Execution Modes:** Tests can run in headed (`--headed`), debug (`--debug`), or interactive UI (`--ui`) modes.

While files run in parallel by default, tests within a file run sequentially unless `fullyParallel: true` is set or `test.describe.configure({mode: 'parallel'})` is used. Inter-dependent tests can be run in `serial` mode. Large suites can be split across machines using the `--shard` flag.
*   **Resource Management:** The `--workers` (or `-j`) flag manages parallelization, and `--max-failures` (or `-x`) stops execution after a specific number of failures.

### Configuration and Setup
Configuration is managed via `defineConfig` in `playwright.config.ts`.
*   **General Settings:** Options include `testDir`, `outputDir`, `timeout` (default 30s), `retries`, and `webServer` for launching local servers.
*   **Global Lifecycle:** Global setup and teardown can be handled via `globalSetup`/`globalTeardown` config options or the recommended Project Dependencies method, which supports fixtures and trace recording.
*   **Browser Management:** `npx playwright install` manages browsers and dependencies, while `npx playwright clear-cache` clears caches.

### Assertions and Annotations
*   **Assertions:** Playwright uses the `expect` function.
    *   **Auto-retrying (Async):** Web-specific matchers (e.g., `toBeVisible()`) that retry until a timeout (default 5s) is reached.
    *   **Non-retrying (Generic):** Standard matchers (e.g., `toBe()`, `toEqual()`) for general conditions.
    *   **Advanced Features:** Includes soft assertions (`expect.soft()`), custom error messages, `expect.poll` for async polling, `expect.toPass` for retrying code blocks, and `expect.extend` for custom matchers.
*   **Annotations:** Tests can be marked with `test.skip()`, `test.fail()`, `test.fixme()`, or `test.slow()` (which triples the timeout). `test.only()` focuses execution on specific tests.

### Fixtures
Fixtures provide isolated environments for tests, offering better encapsulation and reusability than traditional hooks.
*   **Built-in Fixtures:** Include `page`, `context`, `browser`, `browserName`, and `request`.
*   **Custom Fixtures:** Created via `test.extend()`. They can be test-scoped or worker-scoped (`{ scope: 'worker' }`), and can be set to run automatically (`{ auto: true }`) or as declarative options (`{ option: true }`).

### Specialized Tools and Component Testing
*   **CLI Tools:** `codegen` records user actions to generate tests; `show-report` and `show-trace` are used for analysis; `merge-reports` combines blob reports.
*   **Component Testing:** Experimental support for React and Vue allows components to run in real browsers while tests run in Node.js. This includes a `mount` fixture for DOM injection, `update` and `unmount` methods, and `beforeMount`/`afterMount` hooks. An experimental `router` fixture is available for network interception.

### **TestInfo**
This class provides methods to manage the state and output of a currently running test:
*   **`attach(name, options)`**: Attaches a file from disk (via `path`) or a value (via `body`) to the test. These are mutually exclusive. It handles copying files for reporters, allowing the original to be removed after the call.
*   **`fail()` / `fail(condition, description)`**: Marks a test as "should fail," either unconditionally or based on a condition.
*   **`skip()` / `skip(condition, description)`**: Immediately aborts and skips the current test, either unconditionally or based on a condition.
*   **`slow()` / `slow(condition)`**: Marks a test as "slow," which triples its default timeout.
*   **`setTimeout(timeout)`**: Changes the test timeout in milliseconds (0 for no timeout).
*   **`outputPath(...pathSegments)`**: Returns a path within the test's output directory. The resulting path must remain within `testInfo.outputDir` or it will throw an error.

### **TestStepInfo**
This class manages individual test steps:
*   **`attach(name, options)`**: Similar to `testInfo.attach`, but attributes the attachment specifically to the test step rather than the overall test level.
*   **`skip()` / `skip(condition, description)`**: Aborts the current step and marks it as skipped.

### **TestOptions**
This class defines configuration properties for tests:
*   **`acceptDownloads`**: A boolean (defaults to `true`) that determines if attachments are automatically downloaded.
*   **`actionTimeout`**: The default timeout in milliseconds for Playwright actions (defaults to 0).
*   **`baseURL`**: A base URL used to construct full URLs for navigation and request methods (e.g., `page.goto()`).
*   **`browserName`**: Specifies the browser to run tests in (`'chromium'`, `'firefox'`, or `'webkit'`), defaulting to `'chromium'`.
*   **`bypassCSP`**: A boolean (defaults to `false`) that toggles the bypassing of the page's Content-Security-Policy.

It can be used within a test body, `beforeEach` (affecting the shared test timeout), `beforeAll` or `afterAll` (affecting only the hook's timeout), or via `test.describe.configure` for an entire group.

### TestInfo
This class provides methods to manage the status and output of a running test:

*   **Test Status Management:**
    *   **`fail(condition, description)`**: Conditionally marks a test as "should fail" if the boolean condition is true. An optional description can be added for the test report.
    *   **`fixme(condition, description)`**: Conditionally marks a test as "fixme" if the boolean condition is true, which immediately aborts the test. An optional description can be included.
    *   **`slow(condition, description)`**: Conditionally marks a test as "slow" if the boolean condition is true, granting it triple the default timeout. An optional description can be included.
*   **Path Management:**
    *   **`outputPath(...pathSegments)`**: Returns a path within the `testInfo.outputDir` for temporary files, ensuring parallel tests do not interfere. The path must remain within the output directory or it will throw an error.
    *   **`snapshotPath(name, options)`**: Returns the path to a snapshot file. The `kind` option can be specified as `'screenshot'`, `'aria'`, or `'snapshot'` to obtain specific paths for different types of assertions.

### TestInfoError
This class describes the properties available when an error occurs during a test:

*   **`message`**: The error message, set when an `Error` or its subclass is thrown.
*   **`stack`**: The error stack, set when an `Error` or its subclass is thrown.
*   **`value`**: The value that was thrown if it was not an instance of `Error` or its subclass.
*   **`cause`**: The cause of the error, provided it is an instance of `Error`; otherwise, it is `undefined`.
*   **`errorContext`**: Provides additional context for the error, such as an aria snapshot of the receiver during an `expect(...)` matcher failure.

Playwright is a testing framework with extensive capabilities for organizing, executing, and configuring tests.

**Test Organization and Execution**
Tests can be grouped using `test.describe()`, which supports various execution modes such as `parallel` (separate processes) and `serial` (where a failure stops subsequent tests). Specialized groups include `fixme`, `only`, and `skip`, while `test.describe.configure()` manages group-specific timeouts and retries. Setup and teardown are handled via `beforeAll`, `afterAll`, `beforeEach`, and `afterEach` hooks. At the test level, users can focus tests with `test.only`, disable them with `test.skip` or `test.fixme`, and adjust timing using `test.setTimeout` or `test.slow`. Additionally, `test.step` allows for named, nested steps, and `test.extend` and `test.use` facilitate the creation and override of custom fixtures.

**Configuration**
Using `TestConfig` and `defineConfig`, users can manage:
*   **Execution**: Global timeouts, retries, `repeatEach`, and `shard` for multi-machine splitting.
*   **Discovery**: Filtering tests via `testDir`, `testMatch`, `testIgnore`, and `grep`.
*   **Infrastructure**: Managing the maximum number of concurrent `workers`, global setup/teardown files, and launching web servers with readiness checks and shutdown signals.
*   **Output**: Configuring `reporter`, `outputDir`, `preserveOutput`, and `captureGitInfo`.
*   **Build**: Transpiler settings via `tsconfig` and `build`.

**Assertions and Snapshots**
The framework provides global settings for `expect` and async matchers. Snapshot locations are managed via `snapshotPathTemplate`. Assertions include `toMatchSnapshot` and `toHaveScreenshot` (customizable by `threshold`, `maxDiffPixels`, and `maxDiffPixelRatio`), as well as `toMatchAriaSnapshot` for configuring children.

**API Classes, Selectors, and Visual Tools**
The test hierarchy and metadata are managed by `Suite`, `TestCase`, and `TestConfig` classes, while `TestError` provides detailed error stacks and code snippets. Custom selector engines can be created via `register`, and the default `data-testid` can be changed using `setTestIdAttribute`. For visual recording, the `screencast` class enables video recording, frame capture, and annotations such as `showActions()`, `showOverlay()`, and `showChapter()`.

### Browser Class
The `Browser` class manages the browser application and provides several methods for control and debugging:
*   **Page and Context Management:** Production code and testing frameworks are advised to use `browser.newContext()` followed by `browserContext.newPage()` to control lifetimes. The `browser.newPage()` method accepts optional arguments such as `baseURL` (for building URLs in navigation and routing), `acceptDownloads` (defaults to `true`), `bypassCSP` (defaults to `false`), and `clientCertificates` for TLS Client Authentication.
*   **Tracing:** `browser.startTracing()` and `browser.stopTracing()` control Chromium-specific low-level debugging. Tracing can include screenshots of a specific page and be written to a specified file path.
*   **Utility Methods:** 
    *   `removeAllListeners()`: Removes listeners of a specific type or all registered listeners, with options to wait for async listeners or ignore errors.
    *   `unbind()`: Unbinds a previously bound browser server.
    *   `version()`: Returns the browser version.
*   **Events:** The browser emits `context` when a new browser context is created and `disconnected` when the browser application is closed, crashed, or `browser.close()` is called.

### BrowserContext Class
The `BrowserContext` class represents an isolated session within a browser:
*   **Page and State Management:** 
    *   `newPage()`: Creates a new page.
    *   `pages()`: Returns all open pages in the context.
    *   `clearCookies()`: Removes cookies, optionally using filters for name, domain, or path.
*   **Scripting and Functions:** 
    *   `addInitScript()`: Evaluates a script (via function, path, or content) in all pages of the context.
    *   `exposeFunction()` and `exposeBinding()`: Add functions to the `window` object of every frame in every page, allowing the page to call functions in the Playwright context.
*   **Network and Permissions:** 
    *   `route()`: Modifies network requests matching a URL pattern or regex. It can abort, fulfill, or continue requests.
    *   `grantPermissions()`: Grants specific permissions to the context or a specific origin.
*   **Properties:** The context provides access to `clock` (for mocking time), `debugger` (for pausing/resuming execution), `request` (API testing helper using context cookies), and `tracing`.
*   **Events and Waiting:** 
    *   `waitForEvent()`: Waits for a specific event to occur, with optional predicates and timeouts.
    *   Events include `close` (emitted when the context or browser closes) and `console` (emitted when JavaScript calls console API methods).
    *   `removeAllListeners()`: Similar to the Browser class, it manages the removal of event listeners.

The provided text details several methods available within the `page` class of the Playwright API:

**Event and State Management**
*   **`waitForEvent`**: Waits for a specific event (e.g., 'download' or 'popup'). It accepts an event name and optional options or a predicate function to determine when the waiting should resolve.
*   **`waitForLoadState`**: Waits for the page to reach a specific load state. Options include `'load'` (default), `'domcontentloaded'`, and `'networkidle'` (which is discouraged for testing).
*   **`waitForRequest`**: Waits for a matching request based on a URL or a predicate function.
*   **`waitForFunction`**: Resolves when a provided page function returns a truthy value, which can be used to observe changes like viewport size.
*   **`waitForSelector`**: (Discouraged) Waits for an element to satisfy a specific state (appear/disappear or become visible/hidden). The use of Locators and web-first assertions is recommended instead.

**Page Maintenance and Cleanup**
*   **`removeAllListeners`**: Removes listeners for a specific event type. It includes a `behavior` option to determine if the system should `'wait'` for current listener calls to finish, `'ignoreErrors'`, or use the `'default'` behavior.
*   **`removeLocatorHandler`**: Removes all locator handlers previously added via `page.addLocatorHandler()` for a specific locator.
*   **`requestGC`**: Requests the page to perform garbage collection, which is primarily useful for detecting memory leaks using `WeakRef`.

### Stepping through your tests​ {#stepping-through-your-tests}

You can play, pause or step through each action of your test using the toolbar at the top of the Inspector. You can see the current action highlighted in the test code, and matching elements highlighted in the browser window.

### Run a test from a specific breakpoint​ {#run-a-test-from-a-specific-breakpoint}

To speed up the debugging process you can add a
page.pause() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-pause)
method to your test. This way you won't have to step through each action of your test to get to the point where you want to debug.


`awaitpage.pause();`


Once you add a
`page.pause()`
call, run your tests in debug mode. Clicking the "Resume" button in the Inspector will run the test and only stop on the
`page.pause()`
.

### Live editing locators​ {#live-editing-locators}

While running in debug mode you can live edit the locators. Next to the 'Pick Locator' button there is a field showing the
locator (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
that the test is paused on. You can edit this locator directly in the
Pick Locator
field, and matching elements will be highlighted in the browser window.

### Picking locators​ {#picking-locators}

While debugging, you might need to choose a more resilient locator. You can do this by clicking on the
Pick Locator
button and hovering over any element in the browser window. While hovering over an element you will see the code needed to locate this element highlighted below. Clicking an element in the browser will add the locator into the field where you can then either tweak it or copy it into your code.

Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing
role, text and test id locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators)
. If Playwright finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient and uniquely identify the target element, so you don't have to worry about failing tests due to locators.

### Actionability logs​ {#actionability-logs}

By the time Playwright has paused on a click action, it has already performed
actionability checks (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
that can be found in the log. This can help you understand what happened during your test and what Playwright did or tried to do. The log tells you if the element was visible, enabled and stable, if the locator resolved to an element, scrolled into view, and so much more. If actionability can't be reached, it will show the action as pending.

The provided text details several methods within the Playwright `test` class:

*   **`test.only`**: Declares a focused test. When focused tests or suites are present, only those are executed. It accepts a title, optional details (including tags and annotations), and a test body.
*   **`test.setTimeout`**: Changes the timeout for a test, hook, or group. A value of zero indicates no timeout. It can be used within a test body, `beforeEach` (affecting the shared test timeout), `beforeAll` or `afterAll` (affecting only the hook's timeout), or via `test.describe.configure` for an entire group.
*   **`test.skip`**: Used to skip tests that are not intended to be run. Tests can be declared as skipped via `test.skip(title, body)`, skipped at runtime based on a condition or callback, or skipped entirely by calling `test.skip()` inside a test body. It can also be used to skip all tests in a file or `test.describe` group.
*   **`test.slow`**: Marks a test as "slow," which triples the default timeout. This method cannot be used in `beforeAll` or `afterAll` hooks; `test.setTimeout` should be used instead.
*   **`test.step.skip`**: Temporarily disables the execution of a specific test step. It takes a title, a body, and optional options such as `box` (for report formatting), `location`, and `timeout`. The use of `testStepInfo.skip()` is recommended over this method.
*   **`test.use`**: Specifies options or fixtures (such as `locale`) for a single test file or a `test.describe` group. It can be called in the global scope or inside `test.describe`, but calling it within `beforeEach` or `beforeAll` results in an error. Fixtures can also be overridden by providing a function.

Playwright is a testing framework with extensive capabilities for organizing, executing, and configuring tests.

**Test Organization and Execution**
Tests can be grouped using `test.describe()`, which supports various execution modes such as `parallel` (separate processes) and `serial` (where a failure stops subsequent tests). Specialized groups include `fixme`, `only`, and `skip`, while `test.describe.configure()` manages group-specific timeouts and retries. Setup and teardown are handled via `beforeAll`, `afterAll`, `beforeEach`, and `afterEach` hooks. At the test level, users can focus tests with `test.only`, disable them with `test.skip` or `test.fixme`, and adjust timing using `test.setTimeout` or `test.slow`. Additionally, `test.step` allows for named, nested steps, and `test.extend` and `test.use` facilitate the creation and override of custom fixtures.

**Configuration**
Using `TestConfig` and `defineConfig`, users can manage:
*   **Execution**: Global timeouts, retries, `repeatEach`, and `shard` for multi-machine splitting.
*   **Discovery**: Filtering tests via `testDir`, `testMatch`, `testIgnore`, and `grep`.
*   **Infrastructure**: Managing the maximum number of concurrent `workers`, global setup/teardown files, and launching web servers with readiness checks and shutdown signals.
*   **Output**: Configuring `reporter`, `outputDir`, `preserveOutput`, and `captureGitInfo`.
*   **Build**: Transpiler settings via `tsconfig` and `build`.

**Assertions and Snapshots**
The framework provides global settings for `expect` and async matchers. Snapshot locations are managed via `snapshotPathTemplate`. Assertions include `toMatchSnapshot` and `toHaveScreenshot` (customizable by `threshold`, `maxDiffPixels`, and `maxDiffPixelRatio`), as well as `toMatchAriaSnapshot` for configuring children.

**API Classes, Selectors, and Visual Tools**
The test hierarchy and metadata are managed by `Suite`, `TestCase`, and `TestConfig` classes, while `TestError` provides detailed error stacks and code snippets. Custom selector engines can be created via `register`, and the default `data-testid` can be changed using `setTestIdAttribute`. For visual recording, the `screencast` class enables video recording, frame capture, and annotations such as `showActions()`, `showOverlay()`, and `showChapter()`.

user_input: My e2e tests mutate shared server state and run in parallel. What auth model avoids collisions, and how do workers stay on separate accounts?
reference: Give each parallel worker its own account and authenticate it once with a worker-scoped fixture. Key the account on the worker's parallelIndex — which stays the same even when a worker restarts — so a worker always maps to the same account.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state . In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

llm_response:
For tests that modify shared server-side state and run in parallel, the recommended approach is to use one account per parallel worker.

Workers stay on separate accounts by using a worker-scoped fixture that leverages `testInfo.parallelIndex` as a unique identifier for each worker. This allows the system to:
1.  Differentiate between workers.
2.  Assign a unique account to each worker (either by creating a new one or using a list of precreated accounts).
3.  Save and reuse a unique authentication state file for each worker (e.g., using the `parallelIndex` in the filename) within the project's output directory.

Playwright provides comprehensive capabilities for API testing, authentication, and test isolation:

**API Testing**
Users can interact with REST APIs using `APIRequestContext`, which is useful for validating server APIs, setting up server-side state before UI tests, or verifying post-conditions. Configuration options include setting a `baseURL`, proxy settings, and `extraHTTPHeaders`. While a built-in `request` fixture is available, users can also manually create contexts via `apiRequest.newContext()`. These requests can be isolated or associated with a `BrowserContext` to automatically share and update cookies.

**Authentication**
To avoid repeating authentication for every test, Playwright can save authenticated state (IndexedDB, local storage, and cookies) to a file using `storageState()`. 
*   **Strategies:** A shared account is recommended for tests without server-side state, while using one account per worker (via `testInfo.parallelIndex`) is recommended for tests that modify server-side state.
*   **Advanced Use Cases:** Users can authenticate via API for speed, manage multiple roles by applying different `storageState` files, or test interactions between roles using multiple `BrowserContext`s. 
*   **Session Storage:** Because Playwright does not natively persist session storage, it must be handled manually using `page.evaluate` and `context.addInitScript`.
*   **Resetting State:** Authentication can be bypassed for specific tests by resetting the storage state.

**Test Isolation**
Playwright ensures tests run independently by executing them in isolated "browser contexts," which function like incognito profiles with their own cookies, session storage, and local storage. This approach prevents cascading failures and state leakage, removing the need to worry about test order during sharding or parallel execution. 

Beyond isolation, browser contexts allow for:
*   **Multi-User Scenarios:** Creating multiple contexts (e.g., admin and user) within a single test.
*   **Emulation:** Simulating specific permissions, mobile devices, color schemes, and locales.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this
`playwright/.auth`
directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.

danger
The browser state file may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account. We strongly discourage checking them into private or public repositories.

## Basic: shared account in all tests​ {#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

Details

Create
`tests/auth.setup.ts`
that will prepare authenticated browser state for all other tests.

tests/auth.setup.ts

`import{testassetup,expect}from'@playwright/test';importpathfrom'path';constauthFile=path.join(__dirname,'../playwright/.auth/user.json');setup('authenticate',async({page})=>{// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('username');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:authFile});});`

### Session storage​ {#session-storage}

Reusing authenticated state covers
cookies (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Cookies)
,
local storage (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Storage)
and
IndexedDB (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IndexedDB_API)
based authentication. Rarely,
session storage (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/sessionStorage)
is used for storing information associated with the signed-in state. Session storage is specific to a particular domain and is not persisted across page loads. Playwright does not provide API to persist session storage, but the following snippet can be used to save/load session storage.


`// Get session storage and store as env variableconstsessionStorage=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>JSON.stringify(sessionStorage));fs.writeFileSync('playwright/.auth/session.json',sessionStorage,'utf-8');// Set session storage in a new contextconstsessionStorage=JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('playwright/.auth/session.json','utf-8'));awaitcontext.addInitScript(storage=>{if(window.location.hostname==='example.com'){for(const[key,value]ofObject.entries(storage))window.sessionStorage.setItem(key,value);}},sessionStorage);`

user_input: On CI I only want a trace when a test actually fails, and then a way to dig into it. How do retries and tracing fit together?
reference: Enable retries and capture the trace on the first retry (trace: 'on-first-retry'); every retried test then drops a trace.zip. Open those in Trace Viewer to walk the failed run action by action, with DOM, console and network.
reference_contexts: Playwright supports test retries . When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.

Traces should be run on continuous integration on the first retry of a failed test by setting the trace: 'on-first-retry' option in the test configuration file. This will produce a trace.zip file for each test that was retried.
Traces are a great way for debugging your tests when they fail on CI. You can open traces locally or in your browser on trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev) .
llm_response:
On CI, you can configure traces to be recorded only when a test fails by using the `trace: 'on-first-retry'` option in your test configuration file. This setup ensures that a `trace.zip` file is produced specifically for tests that are retried after an initial failure.

To implement this, you can set your configuration as follows:
*   **Retries**: Set `retries` to a value (e.g., 2 when running on CI).
*   **Trace Option**: Set `trace: 'on-first-retry'`.

Under this configuration, traces are recorded on the first retry of a failed test, but not on the first run or subsequent retries. Alternatively, if you do not enable retries but still want traces for failed tests, you can use `trace: 'retain-on-failure'`, which records a trace for every test but removes it from successful runs.

To dig into the failure, you can:
1.  **Open the HTML report**: Run `npx playwright show-report` and click the trace icon next to the test file or open the trace from the 'Traces' tab in the detailed test view.
2.  **Use the CLI**: Open a saved trace using `npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`.
3.  **Use the Browser**: Upload the `trace.zip` file to `trace.playwright.dev`.
llm_references:
`'on-all-retries'`
- Record traces for all test retries.
`'off'`
- Do not record a trace.
`'on'`
- Record a trace for each test. (not recommended as it's performance heavy)
`'retain-on-failure'`
- Record a trace for each test, but remove it from successful test runs.

You can also use
`trace: 'retain-on-failure'`
if you do not enable retries but still want traces for failed tests.

There are more granular options available, see
testOptions.trace (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testoptions#test-options-trace)
.

If you are not using Playwright as a Test Runner, use the
browserContext.tracing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-tracing)
API instead.

## Trace Viewer features​ {#trace-viewer-features}

### Actions​ {#actions}

In the Actions tab you can see what locator was used for every action and how long each one took to run. Hover over each action of your test and visually see the change in the DOM snapshot. Go back and forward in time and click an action to inspect and debug. Use the Before and After tabs to visually see what happened before and after the action.

Selecting each action reveals:

Action snapshots
Action log
Source code location

### Screenshots​ {#screenshots}

When tracing with the
screenshots (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-tracing#tracing-start-option-screenshots)
option turned on (default), each trace records a screencast and renders it as a film strip. You can hover over the film strip to see a magnified image of for each action and state which helps you easily find the action you want to inspect.

Double click on an action to see the time range for that action. You can use the slider in the timeline to increase the actions selected and these will be shown in the Actions tab and all console logs and network logs will be filtered to only show the logs for the actions selected.

### Snapshots​ {#snapshots}

The provided text details the API specifications for `Tracing` and `WebError` classes in Playwright.

### Tracing API
The Tracing API allows for recording actions and network activity within a `BrowserContext`.

*   **`tracing.start()`**: Initiates tracing. Optional arguments include:
    *   `live`: Writes traces to an unarchived file in real time (v1.59).
    *   `name`: Sets a prefix for intermediate trace files.
    *   `screenshots`: Captures screenshots for a timeline preview.
    *   `snapshots`: Records network activity and DOM snapshots on every action.
    *   `sources`: Includes source files for trace actions (v1.17).
    *   `title`: Sets the trace name for the Trace Viewer (v1.17).
*   **`tracing.stop()`**: Stops tracing and can optionally export the trace to a specific `path`.
*   **Trace Chunks**: `tracing.startChunk()` and `tracing.stopChunk()` (added in v1.15) allow for recording multiple separate traces within the same `BrowserContext`. `startChunk` accepts optional `name` (v1.32) and `title` (v1.17) arguments.
*   **HAR Recording**: `tracing.startHar()` (v1.60) records network activity into an HTTP Archive (HAR) file. 
    *   It requires a `path` and supports options for `content` (omit, embed, or attach), `mode` (full or minimal), `resourcesDir` (for attached content), and a `urlFilter` (glob or regex).
    *   Recording is stopped via `tracing.stopHar()` or by disposing of the returned `Disposable`.

### WebError API
The `WebError` class provides information regarding unhandled exceptions.

*   **`error()`**: Returns the unhandled error that was thrown (v1.38).
*   **`location()`**: Returns an object containing the `url` of the resource, as well as the 0-based `line` and `column` numbers (v1.60).
*   **`page()`**: Returns the `Page` that produced the exception, or `null` if none (v1.38).
