`constslowExpect=expect.configure({timeout:10000});awaitslowExpect(locator).toHaveText('Submit');// Always do soft assertions.constsoftExpect=expect.configure({soft:true});awaitsoftExpect(locator).toHaveText('Submit');`


## expect.poll​ {#expectpoll}

You can convert any synchronous
`expect`
to an asynchronous polling one using
`expect.poll`
.

The following method will poll given function until it returns HTTP status 200:


`awaitexpect.poll(async()=>{constresponse=awaitpage.request.get('https://api.example.com');returnresponse.status();},{// Custom expect message for reporting, optional.message:'make sure API eventually succeeds',// Poll for 10 seconds; defaults to 5 seconds. Pass 0 to disable timeout.timeout:10000,}).toBe(200);`


You can also specify custom polling intervals:


`awaitexpect.poll(async()=>{constresponse=awaitpage.request.get('https://api.example.com');returnresponse.status();},{// Probe, wait 1s, probe, wait 2s, probe, wait 10s, probe, wait 10s, probe// ... Defaults to [100, 250, 500, 1000].intervals:[1_000,2_000,10_000],timeout:60_000}).toBe(200);`


You can combine
`expect.configure({ soft: true })`
with expect.poll to perform soft assertions in polling logic.


`constsoftExpect=expect.configure({soft:true});awaitsoftExpect.poll(async()=>{constresponse=awaitpage.request.get('https://api.example.com');returnresponse.status();},{}).toBe(200);`


This allows the test to continue even if the assertion inside poll fails.

## expect.toPass​ {#expecttopass}

You can retry blocks of code until they are passing successfully.


`awaitexpect(async()=>{constresponse=awaitpage.request.get('https://api.example.com');expect(response.status()).toBe(200);}).toPass();`


You can also specify custom timeout and retry intervals:


`awaitexpect(async()=>{constresponse=awaitpage.request.get('https://api.example.com');expect(response.status()).toBe(200);}).toPass({// Probe, wait 1s, probe, wait 2s, probe, wait 10s, probe, wait 10s, probe// ... Defaults to [100, 250, 500, 1000].intervals:[1_000,2_000,10_000],timeout:60_000});`

user_input: What's the reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element, and why avoid xpath=.. for it?
reference: Filter the parent by the child locator — e.g. getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child }) — which is evaluated relative to the parent match. xpath=.. works but is brittle: any DOM change can break it, so prefer filtering.
reference_contexts: The filtering locator must be relative to the original locator and is queried starting with the original locator match, not the document root.

Alternatively, if you cannot find a suitable locator for the parent element, use xpath=.. . Note that this method is not as reliable, because any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests. Prefer locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) when possible.

To select a parent element based on a child element, the recommended approach is to filter by another locator. Specifically, you can prefix a chained selector with an asterisk (`*`) to capture elements queried by an intermediate selector. For example, `*css=article >> text=Hello` captures the `article` element that contains an element with the text "Hello".

## Label to form control retargeting​ {#label-to-form-control-retargeting}

warning
We recommend
locating by label text (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-label)
instead of relying to label-to-control retargeting.

Targeted input actions in Playwright automatically distinguish between labels and controls, so you can target the label to perform an action on the associated control.

For example, consider the following DOM structure:
`<label for="password">Password:</label><input id="password" type="password">`
. You can target the label by its "Password" text using
page.getByText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-text)
. However, the following actions will be performed on the input instead of the label:

locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click)
will click the label and automatically focus the input field;
locator.fill() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-fill)
will fill the input field;
locator.inputValue() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-input-value)
will return the value of the input field;
locator.selectText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-text)
will select text in the input field;
locator.setInputFiles() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-set-input-files)
will set files for the input field with
`type=file`
;
locator.selectOption() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-option)
will select an option from the select box.


`// Fill the input by targeting the label.awaitpage.getByText('Password').fill('secret');`


However, other methods will target the label itself, for example
expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text)
will assert the text content of the label, not the input field.


`// Fill the input by targeting the label.awaitexpect(page.locator('label')).toHaveText('Password');`


## Legacy text locator​ {#legacy-text-locator}

warning
We recommend the modern
text locator (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#get-by-text)
instead.

Legacy text locator matches elements that contain passed text.


`awaitpage.locator('text=Log in').click();`

`css=article >> css=.bar > .baz >> css=span[attr=value]`


is equivalent to


`document.querySelector('article').querySelector('.bar > .baz').querySelector('span[attr=value]');`


If a selector needs to include
`>>`
in the body, it should be escaped inside a string to not be confused with chaining separator, e.g.
`text="some >> text"`
.

### Intermediate matches​ {#intermediate-matches}

warning
We recommend
filtering by another locator (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#filter-by-childdescendant)
to locate elements that contain other elements.

By default, chained selectors resolve to an element queried by the last selector. A selector can be prefixed with
`*`
to capture elements that are queried by an intermediate selector.

For example,
`css=article >> text=Hello`
captures the element with the text
`Hello`
, and
`*css=article >> text=Hello`
(note the
`*`
) captures the
`article`
element that contains some element with the text
`Hello`
.

Playwright utilizes locators as the primary mechanism for finding web elements, featuring built-in auto-waiting and retry-ability. 

**Locators and Selection**
Recommended locators prioritize accessibility and resilience:
*   **Prioritized Methods:** `getByRole()` (mimics user perception), `getByLabel()`, `getByPlaceholder()`, `getByText()`, `getByAltText()`, `getByTitle()`, and `getByTestId()` (most resilient).
*   **Discouraged Methods:** `page.locator()` for CSS/XPath, as they are unstable during DOM changes.
*   **Advanced Selection:** Locators can be pierce shadow roots (except XPath and closed-mode roots), be chained to find nested elements, or combined using `.and()` for multiple criteria and `.or()` for `.or()` for alternative elements.
*   **Filtering:** The `.filter()` method allows narrowing searches based on text (`hasText`, `hasNotText`) or other locators (`has`, `hasNot`), and visibility (`visible: true`).

**User Interactions**
*   **Input:** `fill()` is recommended for text, while `pressSequentially()` simulates real typing and `press()` handles single keystrokes or shortcuts.
*   **Actions:** Standard clicks are available, along with `dispatchEvent('click')` for programmatic clicks. `setInputFiles()` handles file uploads, while `dragTo()` performs drag-and-drop sequences (with lower-level mouse methods for precise control).
*   **Navigation and Focus:** `locator.focus()` handles focus events, and while scrolling is typically automatic, manual options include `scrollIntoViewIfNeeded()`, `mouse.wheel()`, and `locator.evaluate()`.

**Handling Lists and Strictness**
*   **Lists:** Elements can be iterated via `.all()` or `.count()` and `.nth()`, and DOM APIs can be executed via `locator.evaluateAll()`. Specific items can be retrieved by text, test ID, or index (`first()`, `last()`, `last()`, `nth()`), though index-based selection is cautioned against.
*   **Strictness:** Locators are strict by default, throwing exceptions if an operation expecting a single element matches multiple. This is unique locators are the best practice, though users can opt-out of strictness using `.first()`, `.last()`, `nth()`, or `.filter({visible: true})`.

user_input: I'm adopting Page Object Models — how do I wire them so each test gets a ready-to-use page object without boilerplate?
reference: Wrap the POM in a fixture created with test.extend(): the fixture builds the page object (and can do setup/teardown around it), and any test just lists it as an argument. Fixtures are reusable across files, so every spec shares it.
reference_contexts: Page objects simplify authoring by creating a higher-level API which suits your application and simplify maintenance by capturing element selectors in one place and create reusable code to avoid repetition.
To create your own fixture, use test.extend() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-extend) to create a new test object that will include it.
llm_response:
To provide each test with a ready-to-use page object without boilerplate, you can use Playwright's fixture system by extending the base `test` object.

Instead of instantiating page objects within every test, you can create a custom `test` object using `test.extend()`. In this extension, you define your page objects as fixtures. For example, you can create a `todoPage` fixture that:
1. Instantiates the `TodoPage` class using the provided `page` fixture.
2. Performs necessary setup, such as navigating to the URL (`await todoPage.goto()`) or adding initial data.
3. Passes the initialized page object to the test using `await use(todoPage)`.
4. Performs any required cleanup after the test finishes (e.g., `await todoPage.removeAll()`).

Once this custom `test` object is exported and used in your test files, you simply mention the page object fixture in the test function's arguments. The test runner will then automatically handle the setup and teardown, providing a ready-to-use page object directly to the test.

# Page object models | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/pom/>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Large test suites can be structured to optimize ease of authoring and maintenance. Page object models are one such approach to structure your test suite.

A page object represents a part of your web application. An e-commerce web application might have a home page, a listings page and a checkout page. Each of them can be represented by page object models.

Page objects
simplify authoring
by creating a higher-level API which suits your application and
simplify maintenance
by capturing element selectors in one place and create reusable code to avoid repetition.

## Implementation​ {#implementation}

We will create a
`PlaywrightDevPage`
helper class to encapsulate common operations on the
`playwright.dev`
page. Internally, it will use the
`page`
object.

Test
Library
playwright-dev-page.ts

`import{expect,typeLocator,typePage}from'@playwright/test';exportclassPlaywrightDevPage{readonly page:Page;readonly getStartedLink:Locator;readonly gettingStartedHeader:Locator;readonly pomLink:Locator;readonly tocList:Locator;constructor(page:Page){this.page=page;this.getStartedLink=page.locator('a',{hasText:'Get started'});this.gettingStartedHeader=page.locator('h1',{hasText:'Installation'});this.pomLink=page.locator('li',{hasText:'Guides',}).locator('a',{hasText:'Page Object Model',});this.tocList=page.locator('article div.markdown ul > li > a');}asyncgoto(){awaitthis.page.goto('https://playwright.dev');}asyncgetStarted(){awaitthis.getStartedLink.first().click();awaitexpect(this.gettingStartedHeader).toBeVisible();}asyncpageObjectModel(){awaitthis.getStarted();awaitthis.pomLink.click();}}`

models/PlaywrightDevPage.js

`classPlaywrightDevPage{/***@param{import('playwright').Page}page*/constructor(page){this.page=page;this.getStartedLink=page.locator('a',{hasText:'Get started'});this.gettingStartedHeader=page.locator('h1',{hasText:'Installation'});this.pomLink=page.locator('li',{hasText:'Playwright Test',}).locator('a',{hasText:'Page Object Model',});this.tocList=page.locator('article div.markdown ul > li > a');}asyncgetStarted(){awaitthis.getStartedLink.first().click();awaitexpect(this.gettingStartedHeader).toBeVisible();}asyncpageObjectModel(){awaitthis.getStarted();awaitthis.pomLink.click();}}module.exports={PlaywrightDevPage};`


Now we can use the
`PlaywrightDevPage`
class in our tests.

Test
Library

`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';import{PlaywrightDevPage}from'./playwright-dev-page';test('getting started should contain table of contents',async({page})=>{constplaywrightDev=newPlaywrightDevPage(page);awaitplaywrightDev.goto();awaitplaywrightDev.getStarted();awaitexpect(playwrightDev.tocList).toHaveText([`How to install Playwright`,`What's installed`,`How to run the example test`,`How to open the HTML test report`,`Write tests using web-first assertions, fixtures and locators`,`Run single or multiple tests; headed mode`,`Generate tests with Codegen`,`View a trace of your tests`,]);});test('should show Page Object Model article',async({page})=>{constplaywrightDev=newPlaywrightDevPage(page);awaitplaywrightDev.goto();awaitplaywrightDev.pageObjectModel();awaitexpect(page.locator('article')).toContainText('Page Object Model is a common pattern');});`

## Overriding fixtures​ {#overriding-fixtures}

In addition to creating your own fixtures, you can also override existing fixtures to fit your needs. Consider the following example which overrides the
`page`
fixture by automatically navigating to the
`baseURL`
:


`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';exportconsttest=base.extend({page:async({baseURL,page},use)=>{awaitpage.goto(baseURL);awaituse(page);},});`


Notice that in this example, the
`page`
fixture is able to depend on other built-in fixtures such as
testOptions.baseURL (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testoptions#test-options-base-url)
. We can now configure
`baseURL`
in the configuration file, or locally in the test file with
test.use() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-use)
.

example.spec.ts

`test.use({baseURL:'https://playwright.dev'});`


Fixtures can also be overridden, causing the base fixture to be completely replaced with something different. For example, we could override the
testOptions.storageState (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testoptions#test-options-storage-state)
fixture to provide our own data.


`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';exportconsttest=base.extend({storageState:async({},use)=>{constcookie=awaitgetAuthCookie();awaituse({cookies:[cookie]});},});`


## Worker-scoped fixtures​ {#worker-scoped-fixtures}

Playwright Test uses
worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
to run test files. Similar to how test fixtures are set up for individual test runs, worker fixtures are set up for each worker process. That's where you can set up services, run servers, etc. Playwright Test will reuse the worker process for as many test files as it can, provided their worker fixtures match and hence environments are identical.

Below we'll create an
`account`
fixture that will be shared by all tests in the same worker, and override the
`page`
fixture to log in to this account for each test. To generate unique accounts, we'll use the
workerInfo.workerIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-workerinfo#worker-info-worker-index)
that is available to any test or fixture. Note the tuple-like syntax for the worker fixture - we have to pass
`{scope: 'worker'}`
so that test runner sets this fixture up once per worker.

In addition to only being run once per worker, worker-scoped fixtures also get a separate timeout equal to the default test timeout. You can change it by passing the
`timeout`
option. See
fixture timeout (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-fixtures/#fixture-timeout)
for more details.

my-test.ts

`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';typeAccount={username:string;password:string;};// Note that we pass worker fixture types as a second template parameter.exportconsttest=base.extend<{},{account:Account}>({account:[async({browser},use,workerInfo)=>{// Unique username.constusername='user'+workerInfo.workerIndex;constpassword='verysecure';// Create the account with Playwright.constpage=awaitbrowser.newPage();awaitpage.goto('/signup');awaitpage.getByLabel('User Name').fill(username);awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);awaitpage.getByText('Sign up').click();// Make sure everything is ok.awaitexpect(page.getByTestId('result')).toHaveText('Success');// Do not forget to cleanup.awaitpage.close();// Use the account value.awaituse({username,password});},{scope:'worker'}],page:async({page,account},use)=>{// Sign in with our account.const{username,password}=account;awaitpage.goto('/signin');awaitpage.getByLabel('User Name').fill(username);awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);awaitpage.getByText('Sign in').click();awaitexpect(page.getByTestId('userinfo')).toHaveText(username);// Use signed-in page in the test.awaituse(page);},});export{expect}from'@playwright/test';`

`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';import{TodoPage}from'./todo-page';// Extend basic test by providing a "todoPage" fixture.consttest=base.extend<{todoPage:TodoPage}>({todoPage:async({page},use)=>{consttodoPage=newTodoPage(page);awaittodoPage.goto();awaittodoPage.addToDo('item1');awaittodoPage.addToDo('item2');awaituse(todoPage);awaittodoPage.removeAll();},});test('should add an item',async({todoPage})=>{awaittodoPage.addToDo('my item');// ...});test('should remove an item',async({todoPage})=>{awaittodoPage.remove('item1');// ...});`

To create your own fixture, use
test.extend() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-extend)
to create a new
`test`
object that will include it.

Below we create two fixtures
`todoPage`
and

# Fixtures | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-fixtures/>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test is based on the concept of test fixtures. Test fixtures are used to establish the environment for each test, giving the test everything it needs and nothing else. Test fixtures are isolated between tests. With fixtures, you can group tests based on their meaning, instead of their common setup.

### Built-in fixtures​ {#built-in-fixtures}

You have already used test fixtures in your first test.


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('basic test',async({page})=>{awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev/');awaitexpect(page).toHaveTitle(/Playwright/);});`


The
`{ page }`
argument tells Playwright Test to set up the
`page`
fixture and provide it to your test function.

Here is a list of the pre-defined fixtures that you are likely to use most of the time:

Fixture
Type
Description
page
Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page)
Isolated page for this test run.
context
BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext)
Isolated context for this test run. The
`page`
fixture belongs to this context as well. Learn how to
configure context (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.
browser
Browser (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browser)
Browsers are shared across tests to optimize resources. Learn how to
configure browsers (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.
browserName
string (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Data_structures#String_type)
The name of the browser currently running the test. Either
`chromium`
,
`firefox`
or
`webkit`
.
request
APIRequestContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext)
Isolated
APIRequestContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext)
instance for this test run.

### Without fixtures​ {#without-fixtures}

Here is how a typical test environment setup differs between the traditional test style and the fixture-based one.

`TodoPage`
is a class that helps us interact with a "todo list" page of the web app, following the
Page Object Model (https://playwright.dev/docs/pom)
pattern. It uses Playwright's
`page`
internally.

llm_response:
Before executing a `locator.click()`, Playwright performs actionability checks to ensure the element behaves as expected. Specifically, it verifies that the locator resolves to a single element and that the element is visible, stable (not animating), and receives events. It also checks if other elements, such as overlays, would capture the click at the target point.

These checks are part of Playwright's auto-waiting functionality. If these actionability checks are not completed within the specified timeout, a `TimeoutError` occurs.
llm_references:
Playwright utilizes auto-waiting to perform actionability checks on elements before executing actions, ensuring they behave as expected. If these checks are not completed within the specified timeout, a `TimeoutError` occurs. For instance, when using `locator.click()`, Playwright verifies that the locator resolves to a single element and that the element is visible, stable (not animating), and receives events. It specifically checks if other elements, such as overlays, would capture the click at the target point.

Certain actions, including `locator.click()`, offer a `force` option. When a truthy value is passed to this option, non-essential actionability checks—such as verifying if the target element receives click events—are disabled.

Additionally, Playwright provides auto-retrying assertions to reduce flakiness by waiting for specific conditions to be met. Available assertions include:
* `toBeAttached()`: Element is attached
* `toBeChecked()`: Checkbox is checked
* `toBeDisabled()`: Element is disabled
* `toBeEditable()`: Element is editable
* `toBeEmpty()`: Container is empty
* `toBeEnabled()`: Element is enabled
* `toBeFocused()`: Element is focused

The provided text details various functionalities of the Playwright `Page` class, focusing on locator handlers and page events.

**Locator Handlers (`page.addLocatorHandler`)**
This feature allows for the handling of overlays that appear during tests.
*   **Behavior:** Playwright checks for the overlay before executing actions that require actionability checks or auto-waiting assertions. If visible, the handler is called before the action/assertion proceeds.
*   **Key Considerations:**
    *   Handlers are only triggered during actions or assertions; they do not trigger if the overlay appears while the test is idle.
    *   The handler's execution time counts toward the action/assertion timeout.
    *   By default, Playwright ensures the overlay is no longer visible after the handler runs, though this can be disabled using `noWaitAfter`.
    *   Multiple handlers can be registered, but only one runs at a time.
    *   Handlers can be automatically removed after a specific number of invocations using the `times` option.
*   **Warnings:** Because handlers alter page state (such as mouse position and element focus), users should avoid sequential actions that rely on unchanged state (e.g., `locator.focus()` followed by `keyboard.press()`). Instead, self-contained actions like `locator.press()` or `locator.click()` are recommended.

**Page Events**
The text describes several events that can be monitored using `page.on()`:
*   **Frame Events:** `framenavigated` (emitted when a frame navigates to a new URL) and `framedetached`.
*   **Page State Events:** `load` (emitted when the JavaScript load event is dispatched) and `popup` (emitted when a new tab or window opens).
*   **Error Events:** `pageerror` (emitted when an uncaught exception occurs within the page).
*   **Network Events:** 
    *   `request`: Emitted when the page issues a request (the request object is read-only).
    *   `requestfailed`: Emitted when a request fails due to client-side issues (e.g., network errors). Note that HTTP error responses (like 404 or 503) are considered successful responses and do not trigger this event.

The provided text outlines several core functionalities of Playwright:

**JavaScript Evaluation**
Playwright distinguishes between the testing environment and the browser page environment. To run JavaScript within the browser context and retrieve results, the `page.evaluate()` API is used. Because these environments are separate, variables from the test must be passed explicitly as arguments to the evaluation function. For setup tasks like mocking data before a page loads, `page.addInitScript()` or `browserContext.addInitScript()` can be utilized.

**Event Handling**
Playwright provides multiple ways to handle web page events (such as network requests or popups):
*   **Waiting:** Using methods like `page.waitForRequest()` or `page.waitForEvent()` to pause execution until a specific event occurs.
*   **Listeners:** Using `page.on()` to handle events that occur at random times and `page.off()` to remove those listeners.
*   **One-off Listeners:** Using `page.once()` for events that only need to be handled a single time.

**Extensibility**
Custom selector engines can be registered via `selectors.register()`. These engines require `query` and `queryAll` functions. They can be run directly in the frame's JavaScript context or as "content scripts" (using the `{contentScript: true}` option) to isolate the engine from the frame's JavaScript for increased safety.

**User Actions and Input**
Playwright can simulate various human interactions with HTML elements:
*   **Text Input:** `locator.fill()` is used for text, date, time, and local datetime inputs.
*   **Selection:** `locator.setChecked()` handles checkboxes and radio buttons, while `locator.selectOption()` manages `<select>` elements.
*   **Mouse Interactions:** Supports generic clicks, double clicks, right clicks, modifier clicks (Shift, Ctrl/Meta), and hovering. 
*   **Click Logic:** Pointer-related methods automatically perform actionability checks (waiting for the element to be in the DOM, displayed, stable, and non-obscured). These checks can be bypassed using `{force: true}` or simulated programmatically via `locator.dispatchEvent('click')`.

The provided text details several methods available within the `page` class of the Playwright API:

**Event and State Management**
*   **`waitForEvent`**: Waits for a specific event (e.g., 'download' or 'popup'). It accepts an event name and optional options or a predicate function to determine when the waiting should resolve.
*   **`waitForLoadState`**: Waits for the page to reach a specific load state. Options include `'load'` (default), `'domcontentloaded'`, and `'networkidle'` (which is discouraged for testing).
*   **`waitForRequest`**: Waits for a matching request based on a URL or a predicate function.
*   **`waitForFunction`**: Resolves when a provided page function returns a truthy value, which can be used to observe changes like viewport size.
*   **`waitForSelector`**: (Discouraged) Waits for an element to satisfy a specific state (appear/disappear or become visible/hidden). The use of Locators and web-first assertions is recommended instead.

**Page Maintenance and Cleanup**
*   **`removeAllListeners`**: Removes listeners for a specific event type. It includes a `behavior` option to determine if the system should `'wait'` for current listener calls to finish, `'ignoreErrors'`, or use the `'default'` behavior.
*   **`removeLocatorHandler`**: Removes all locator handlers previously added via `page.addLocatorHandler()` for a specific locator.
*   **`requestGC`**: Requests the page to perform garbage collection, which is primarily useful for detecting memory leaks using `WeakRef`.

The provided text covers three main areas of Playwright: handling dialogs, using Docker, and managing downloads.

**Dialogs**
Playwright can interact with web page dialogs, including `alert`, `confirm`, `prompt`, and `beforeunload` confirmations. By default, dialogs are auto-dismissed. However, users can register a `page.on('dialog')` listener to either accept or dismiss them. If a listener is registered but does not handle the dialog, the action (such as a click) will stall because dialogs are modals that block page execution. For `beforeunload` dialogs, the `page.close()` method must be invoked with `runBeforeUnload: true`. To assert that a print dialog was triggered via `window.print`, a specific script evaluation and `page.waitForFunction` approach is used.

**Docker**
Playwright provides Docker images (such as `Dockerfile.noble`) that include browsers and system dependencies, though the Playwright package must be installed separately. 
*   **Usage:** Images are available via the Microsoft Artifact Registry. For trusted end-to-end tests, the `root` user is acceptable, but for crawling or scraping untrusted sites, it is recommended to use a separate user with a seccomp profile to enable the Chromium sandbox.
*   **Configuration:** Recommended flags include `--init` to avoid zombie processes and `--ipc=host` to prevent Chromium from running out of memory.
*   **Remote Connection:** A Playwright Server can be run in Docker, allowing tests to connect via an environment variable (`PW_TEST_CONNECT_WS_ENDPOINT`) or the `browserType.connect()` API.
*   **Other Features:** The `noVNC` viewer can be enabled via `desktop-lite` in `devcontainer.json` for recording tests and picking selectors.
*   **Compatibility:** Images are based on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble) and 22.04 LTS (Jammy). Alpine Linux is not supported because Firefox and WebKit builds require the `glibc` library.

**Downloads**
When a page downloads an attachment, a `page.on('download')` event is emitted, and the file is placed in a temporary folder. These files are deleted once the browser context is closed. Users can specify a persistence location using the `downloadsPath` option in `browserType.launch()`. The standard process for handling downloads involves waiting for the `download` event before triggering the download action and then using `download.saveAs()` to persist the file.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

For every attachment downloaded by the page,
page.on('download') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-download)
event is emitted. All these attachments are downloaded into a temporary folder. You can obtain the download url, file name and payload stream using the
Download (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-download)
object from the event.

You can specify where to persist downloaded files using the
downloadsPath (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-launch-option-downloads-path)
option in
browserType.launch() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-launch)
.

note
Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.

Here is the simplest way to handle the file download:


`// Start waiting for download before clicking. Note no await.constdownloadPromise=page.waitForEvent('download');awaitpage.getByText('Download file').click();constdownload=awaitdownloadPromise;// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.awaitdownload.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/'+download.suggestedFilename());`


#### Variations​ {#variations}

If you have no idea what initiates the download, you can still handle the event:


`page.on('download',download=>download.path().then(console.log));`


Note that handling the event forks the control flow and makes the script harder to follow. Your scenario might end while you are downloading a file since your main control flow is not awaiting for this operation to resolve.

The provided text details settings for HAR (HTTP Archive) recording and routing, specifically focusing on resource content management, recording modes, and filtering.

**Resource Content Management**
The 
`content` 
(or `updateContent`) setting controls how resource content is handled:
*   **`omit`**: Content is not persisted.
*   **`embed`**: Content is stored inline within the HAR file as per the HAR specification.
*   **`attach`**: Resources are persisted as separate files or entries in a ZIP archive.
*   **Defaults**: For `.zip` output files, the default is `attach`; for all other file extensions, the default is `embed`. If the file name ends in `.zip`, `content: 'attach'` is used by default.

**Recording and Update Modes**
The `mode` (or `updateMode`) setting determines the amount of information recorded:
*   **`full`**: The default recording mode.
*   **`minimal`**: Records only the information necessary for routing from HAR, omitting sizes, timing, page, cookies, security, and other non-essential replaying information.

**Filtering and Pathing**
*   **`path`**: Specifies the filesystem path where the HAR file is written.
*   **`urlFilter`**: An optional glob or regex pattern used to filter requests stored in the HAR. If a `baseURL` was provided via context options and the URL is a path, it is merged using the `new URL()` constructor.
*   **`url`**: An optional glob pattern, regular expression, or predicate to match request URLs; only matching requests are served from the HAR file.

**Operational Requirements**
*   HAR recording is enabled for all pages into the `recordHar.path` file if specified.
*   To ensure the HAR file is saved and written to disk, `browserContext.close()` must be awaited.

*   **`start()`**: Initiates the screencast. It can be configured with:

*   **Actions**:

The provided text outlines the API methods for Tracing and Video in Playwright.

### Tracing
The `tracing` API captures network activity and browser operations. While `tracing.start` can be used to begin tracing, it is recommended to enable tracing via the Playwright Test configuration to ensure test assertions (like `expect` calls) are included.

Key methods include:
*   **group**: Creates a new group in the trace viewer for subsequent API calls. It accepts a name and optional location details (file, line, and column). Users are encouraged to use `test.step` instead when available.
*   **groupEnd**: Closes the most recently created group.
*   **stopChunk**: Exports the trace collected since the last `startChunk` call to a specified file path.
*   **stopHar**: Stops HAR recording and saves the file to the path provided during `startHar`.

### Video
The `video` API manages video recordings of browser sessions.

Key methods include:
*   **path**: Returns the file system path where the video is being recorded. This method throws an error if connected remotely.
*   **saveAs**: Saves the video to a user-specified path, waiting until the page is closed and the video is fully saved.
*   **delete**: Deletes the video file, waiting for the recording to finish if necessary.

user_input: What's the difference between page.screenshot() and toHaveScreenshot(), and when do I use each?
reference: page.screenshot() simply captures an image to a file or buffer. toHaveScreenshot() is a visual-regression assertion: the first run saves a reference image and later runs compare against it, failing on unexpected differences.
reference_contexts: Here is a quick way to capture a screenshot and save it into a file:

Playwright Test includes the ability to produce and visually compare screenshots using await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() . On first execution, Playwright test will generate reference screenshots. Subsequent runs will compare against the reference.
llm_response:
`page.screenshot()` is used to capture an image of the page and either save it to a file (using the `path` option) or return it as a buffer for post-processing or passing to a third-party pixel diff facility. It can be used for general purposes, such as taking a screenshot of a full scrollable page, a single element, or a specific clip area.

`toHaveScreenshot()` is a screenshot assertion used specifically with the Playwright test runner. It waits until two consecutive page screenshots yield the same result and then compares the final screenshot with an expectation. It includes specialized options for testing, such as `threshold` (perceived color difference), `maxDiffPixels`, `maxDiffPixelRatio`, and `mask` (to overlay specific elements with a colored box to ensure repeatable screenshots).

**When to use each:**
*   Use `page.screenshot()` when you need to capture and save an image of the page or an element for manual review or external processing.
*   Use `toHaveScreenshot()` when you are writing tests and want to automatically verify that the current page appearance matches a baseline expectation.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Here is a quick way to capture a screenshot and save it into a file:


`awaitpage.screenshot({path:'screenshot.png'});`

Full page screenshot is a screenshot of a full scrollable page, as if you had a very tall screen and the page could fit it entirely.


`awaitpage.screenshot({path:'screenshot.png',fullPage:true});`

Rather than writing into a file, you can get a buffer with the image and post-process it or pass it to a third party pixel diff facility.


`constbuffer=awaitpage.screenshot();console.log(buffer.toString('base64'));`


## Element screenshot​ {#element-screenshot}

Sometimes it is useful to take a screenshot of a single element.


`awaitpage.locator('.header').screenshot({path:'screenshot.png'});`

The provided text details the options for taking screenshots using `elementHandle` and describes the `scrollIntoViewIfNeeded` method.

**Screenshot Options:**
*   **Animations:** Finite animations are fast-forwarded to completion (firing the `transitionend` event), while infinite animations are canceled to their initial state and played over after the screenshot. The default is `"allow"`.
*   **Caret:** Can be set to `"hide"` (default) or `"initial"`.
*   **Masking:** Locators can be specified to be masked with a pink box (`#FF00FF` by default), which can be customized using `maskColor`. Masking applies to both visible and invisible elements.
*   **Background and Quality:** `omitBackground` (default `false`) allows for transparency by hiding the white background, though it does not work for `jpeg` images. `quality` (0-100) is available but not applicable to `png` images.
*   **Path and Type:** The `path` option saves the image to a file (relative paths are resolved to the current working directory); otherwise, the image is not saved to disk. The `type` defaults to `"png"` but can be set to `"jpeg"`.
*   **Scale:** Defaults to `"device"` (one pixel per device pixel). Setting it to `"css"` results in one pixel per CSS pixel, keeping screenshots smaller on high-dpi devices.
*   **Style:** Allows applying a stylesheet to hide dynamic elements or change properties for repeatable screenshots. This stylesheet applies to inner frames and pierces the Shadow DOM.
*   **Timeout:** Maximum time in milliseconds, defaulting to `0` (no timeout).

**scrollIntoViewIfNeeded Method:**
This method is discouraged in favor of `locator.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded()`. It waits for actionability checks and scrolls the element into view unless it is already completely visible according to the `IntersectionObserver` ratio. It throws an error if the `elementHandle` is not connected to a ShadowRoot or Document.

user_input: In one test I need an admin and a regular user acting at the same time. How do I get two authenticated sessions side by side?
reference: Open two browser contexts in the same test, each seeded with a different storageState — one admin, one user — and drive their pages independently. Multiple contexts in one scenario is exactly how Playwright models multi-user features like chat, and they stay isolated.
reference_contexts: Use multiple BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext) s and Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page) s with different storage states in the same test.
Playwright can create multiple browser contexts within a single scenario. This is useful when you want to test for multi-user functionality, like a chat.
llm_response:
To have an admin and a regular user acting at the same time in a single test, you can use one of the following two methods:

**1. Using Multiple BrowserContexts and Pages**
You can create multiple `BrowserContext` and `Page` instances within the same test, each utilizing a different storage state. For example:
* Create an `adminContext` using the admin storage state file (e.g., `playwright/.auth/admin.json`) and open an `adminPage` from it.
* Create a `userContext` using the user storage state file (e.g., `playwright/.auth/user.json`) and open a `userPage` from it.
* Interact with both pages simultaneously and close the contexts when finished.

**2. Using POM Fixtures**
You can introduce fixtures that provide a page authenticated as each role. This involves:
* Creating Page Object Models (POMs) for the admin and user pages.
* Extending the `test` object to create fixtures (e.g., `adminPage` and `userPage`) that each initialize a new browser context with the respective storage state and return the corresponding POM.
* Using these fixtures directly in your test (e.g., `test('admin and user', async ({ adminPage, userPage }) => { ... })`) to interact with both authenticated sessions side by side.

### Multiple signed in roles​ {#multiple-signed-in-roles}

When to use

You have more than one role in your end to end tests, but you can reuse accounts across all tests.

Details

We will authenticate multiple times in the setup project.

tests/auth.setup.ts

`import{testassetup,expect}from'@playwright/test';constadminFile='playwright/.auth/admin.json';setup('authenticate as admin',async({page})=>{// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('admin');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:adminFile});});constuserFile='playwright/.auth/user.json';setup('authenticate as user',async({page})=>{// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('user');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:userFile});});`

### Session storage​ {#session-storage}

Reusing authenticated state covers
cookies (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Cookies)
,
local storage (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Storage)
and
IndexedDB (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IndexedDB_API)
based authentication. Rarely,
session storage (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/sessionStorage)
is used for storing information associated with the signed-in state. Session storage is specific to a particular domain and is not persisted across page loads. Playwright does not provide API to persist session storage, but the following snippet can be used to save/load session storage.


`// Get session storage and store as env variableconstsessionStorage=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>JSON.stringify(sessionStorage));fs.writeFileSync('playwright/.auth/session.json',sessionStorage,'utf-8');// Set session storage in a new contextconstsessionStorage=JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('playwright/.auth/session.json','utf-8'));awaitcontext.addInitScript(storage=>{if(window.location.hostname==='example.com'){for(const[key,value]ofObject.entries(storage))window.sessionStorage.setItem(key,value);}},sessionStorage);`

Playwright provides comprehensive capabilities for API testing, authentication, and test isolation:

**API Testing**
Users can interact with REST APIs using `APIRequestContext`, which is useful for validating server APIs, setting up server-side state before UI tests, or verifying post-conditions. Configuration options include setting a `baseURL`, proxy settings, and `extraHTTPHeaders`. While a built-in `request` fixture is available, users can also manually create contexts via `apiRequest.newContext()`. These requests can be isolated or associated with a `BrowserContext` to automatically share and update cookies.

**Authentication**
To avoid repeating authentication for every test, Playwright can save authenticated state (IndexedDB, local storage, and cookies) to a file using `storageState()`. 
*   **Strategies:** A shared account is recommended for tests without server-side state, while using one account per worker (via `testInfo.parallelIndex`) is recommended for tests that modify server-side state.
*   **Advanced Use Cases:** Users can authenticate via API for speed, manage multiple roles by applying different `storageState` files, or test interactions between roles using multiple `BrowserContext`s. 
*   **Session Storage:** Because Playwright does not natively persist session storage, it must be handled manually using `page.evaluate` and `context.addInitScript`.
*   **Resetting State:** Authentication can be bypassed for specific tests by resetting the storage state.

**Test Isolation**
Playwright ensures tests run independently by executing them in isolated "browser contexts," which function like incognito profiles with their own cookies, session storage, and local storage. This approach prevents cascading failures and state leakage, removing the need to worry about test order during sharding or parallel execution. 

Beyond isolation, browser contexts allow for:
*   **Multi-User Scenarios:** Creating multiple contexts (e.g., admin and user) within a single test.
*   **Emulation:** Simulating specific permissions, mobile devices, color schemes, and locales.

, which is automatically cleaned up before every test run.

## Moderate: one account per parallel worker​ {#moderate-one-account-per-parallel-worker}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests that
modify server-side state
. In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

When to use

Your tests modify shared server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting.

When not to use

Your tests do not modify any shared server-side state. In this case, all tests can use a single shared account.

Details

We will authenticate once per
worker process (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#worker-processes)
, each with a unique account.

Create
`playwright/fixtures.ts`
file that will
override storageState fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#overriding-fixtures)
to authenticate once per worker. Use
testInfo.parallelIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-parallel-index)
to differentiate between workers.

playwright/fixtures.ts

`import{testasbaseTest,expect}from'@playwright/test';importfsfrom'fs';importpathfrom'path';export*from'@playwright/test';exportconsttest=baseTest.extend<{},{workerStorageState:string}>({// Use the same storage state for all tests in this worker.storageState:({workerStorageState},use)=>use(workerStorageState),// Authenticate once per worker with a worker-scoped fixture.workerStorageState:[async({browser},use)=>{// Use parallelIndex as a unique identifier for each worker.constid=test.info().parallelIndex;constfileName=path.resolve(test.info().project.outputDir,`.auth/${id}.json`);if(fs.existsSync(fileName)){// Reuse existing authentication state if any.awaituse(fileName);return;}// Important: make sure we authenticate in a clean environment by unsetting storage state.constpage=awaitbrowser.newPage({storageState:undefined});// Acquire a unique account, for example create a new one.// Alternatively, you can have a list of precreated accounts for testing.// Make sure that accounts are unique, so that multiple team members// can run tests at the same time without interference.constaccount=awaitacquireAccount(id);// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill(account.username);awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill(account.password);awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:fileName});awaitpage.close();awaituse(fileName);},{scope:'worker'}],});`

### Authenticate with API request​ {#authenticate-with-api-request}

When to use

Your web application supports authenticating via API that is easier/faster than interacting with the app UI.

llm_response:
When a test fails, Playwright Test discards the entire worker process and the browser, then starts a new worker process to continue testing. Because `beforeAll` and `afterAll` hooks are tied to the worker process, they run again in the new worker.

In serial groups (`test.describe.serial`), the behavior with retries is as follows:
*   **Failure Impact**: If one test in a serial group fails, all subsequent tests in that group are skipped.
*   **Retry Behavior**: When retries are enabled, the entire group is retried together. This means the `beforeAll` hook runs again, and all tests in the group—including those that previously passed—are executed again in order.

### Test Group Declarations (`test.describe`)
Several variations of `test.describe` are available to control how groups of tests are executed:

*   **`test.describe.fixme`**: Marks a group of tests as "fixme," meaning they will not be executed.
*   **`test.describe.only`**: Declares a focused group. If focused tests or suites exist, only they will run.
*   **`test.describe.skip`**: Declares a skipped group; tests within this group are never run.
*   **`test.describe.parallel`**: Executes tests in separate processes. Because they are isolated, they cannot share global variables or state, and each test executes all relevant hooks.
*   **`test.describe.serial`**: Ensures tests run serially. If one test fails, all subsequent tests in the group are skipped, and the group is retried together. This method is discouraged in favor of isolated tests.
*   **Focused Parallel/Serial Groups**: `test.describe.parallel.only` and `test.describe.serial.only` combine focusing logic with their respective execution modes. Both are discouraged in favor of using `test.describe.configure()`.

**Common Arguments for Group Declarations:**
Most of these methods accept a `title` (optional string), `details` (optional object containing `tag` and `annotation` with `type` and `description`), and a `callback` function that is run immediately to define the tests belonging to the group.

### Configuration and Extensions
*   **`test.describe.configure`**: This is the preferred method for configuring execution modes (such as "default", "parallel", or "serial"). It can also be used to set the number of `retries` for each test and a `timeout` in milliseconds, which overrides project and config timeouts.
*   **`test.extend`**: Allows the `test` object to be extended by defining custom fixtures and options. This enables the creation of reusable components (e.g., a `TodoPage` fixture) that can be used across multiple tests.

### Test Hooks
Playwright provides four primary hooks to manage setup and teardown:
*   **`test.beforeAll`**: Executes once per worker process before all tests. If called in a test file, it runs before all tests in that file; if called inside a `test.describe` group, it runs before all tests in that group.
*   **`test.afterAll`**: Used to teardown resources set up in `beforeAll`.
*   **`test.beforeEach`**: Executes before each test in a file or a `test.describe` group. It provides access to fixtures and the `TestInfo` object.
*   **`test.afterEach`**: Executes after each test in a file or a `test.describe` group. It can be used to check test status (e.g., whether a test succeeded or failed).

**General Hook Details:**
*   Hooks can optionally be declared with a **title** (added in v1.38).
*   When multiple hooks of the same type are added, they run in the order of registration.
*   Playwright continues running applicable hooks even if some have failed.
*   For `beforeAll` and `afterAll`, the worker process restarts on test failures, causing these hooks to run again in the new worker.

### Test Grouping
*   **`test.describe`**: Used to declare a group of tests. A title can be provided, which will then appear as part of each test's title in the test report.

### Test Steps
*   **`test.step`**: Allows the creation of named steps within a test. Steps can be nested, and the method returns the value returned by the step callback.
*   **Step Options**:
    *   **`box`**: When set to `true`, errors thrown inside the step point to the step call site rather than the specific internal action that failed.
    *   **`location`**: Specifies a custom location for the step in reports and the trace viewer.
    *   **`timeout`**: Sets a maximum time (in milliseconds) for the step to complete before throwing a `TimeoutError`.
*   **Decorators**: TypeScript method decorators can be used to turn class methods into steps (including boxed steps).
*   **`test.step.skip`**: Temporarily disables the execution of a specific step. While available, `testStepInfo.skip()` is the recommended alternative.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Test retries are a way to automatically re-run a test when it fails. This is useful when a test is flaky and fails intermittently. Test retries are configured in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

## Failures​ {#failures}

Playwright Test runs tests in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

Consider the following snippet:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe('suite',()=>{test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test.afterAll(async()=>{/* ... */});});`


When
all tests pass
, they will run in order in the same worker process.

Worker process starts
`beforeAll`

`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
passes
`third good`
passes
`afterAll`
hook runs

Should
any test fail
, Playwright Test will discard the entire worker process along with the browser and will start a new one. Testing will continue in the new worker process starting with the next test.

Worker process #1 starts
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
fails
`afterAll`
hook runs
Worker process #2 starts
`beforeAll`
hook runs again
`third good`
passes
`afterAll`
hook runs

If you
enable
retries (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-retries/#retries)
, second worker process will start by retrying the failed test and continue from there.

Worker process #1 starts
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
fails
`afterAll`

Worker process #2 starts
`beforeAll`
hook runs again
`second flaky`

`third good`

`afterAll`
hook runs

This scheme works perfectly for independent tests and guarantees that failing tests can't affect healthy ones.

## Retries​ {#retries}

Playwright supports
test retries
. When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.


`# Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsnpx playwrighttest--retries=3`


You can configure retries in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsretries:3,});`


Playwright Test will categorize tests as follows:

"passed" - tests that passed on the first run;
"flaky" - tests that failed on the first run, but passed when retried;
"failed" - tests that failed on the first run and failed all retries.


`Running3tests using1worker✓ example.spec.ts:4:2 › first passes(438ms)x example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky(691ms)✓ example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky(522ms)✓ example.spec.ts:6:2 › third passes(932ms)1flakyexample.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky2passed(4s)`

`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('my test',async({page},testInfo)=>{if(testInfo.retry)awaitcleanSomeCachesOnTheServer();// ...});`

test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)

`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test.describe(()=>{// All tests in this describe group will get 2 retry attempts.test.describe.configure({retries:2});test('test 1',async({page})=>{// ...});test('test 2',async({page})=>{// ...});});`

## Box fixtures​ {#box-fixtures}

Usually, custom fixtures are reported as separate steps in the UI mode, Trace Viewer and various test reports. They also appear in error messages from the test runner. For frequently used fixtures, this can mean lots of noise. You can stop the fixtures steps from being shown in the UI by "boxing" it.


`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';exportconsttest=base.extend({helperFixture:[async({},use,testInfo)=>{// ...},{box:true}],});`


This is useful for non-interesting helper fixtures. For example, an
automatic (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#automatic-fixtures)
fixture that sets up some common data can be safely hidden from a test report.

You can also mark the fixture as
`box: 'self'`
to only hide that particular fixture, but include all the steps inside the fixture in the test report.

## Custom fixture title​ {#custom-fixture-title}

Instead of the usual fixture name, you can give fixtures a custom title that will be shown in test reports and error messages.


`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';exportconsttest=base.extend({innerFixture:[async({},use,testInfo)=>{// ...},{title:'my fixture'}],});`

`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('my test',async({page},testInfo)=>{if(testInfo.retry)awaitcleanSomeCachesOnTheServer();// ...});`

test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.


`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test.describe(()=>{// All tests in this describe group will get 2 retry attempts.test.describe.configure({retries:2});test('test 1',async({page})=>{// ...});test('test 2',async({page})=>{// ...});});`


## Serial mode​ {#serial-mode}

Use
test.describe.serial() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-serial)
to group dependent tests to ensure they will always run together and in order. If one of the tests fails, all subsequent tests are skipped. All tests in the group are retried together.

Consider the following snippet that uses
`test.describe.serial`
:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'serial'});test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


When running without
retries (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-retries/#retries)
, all tests after the failure are skipped:

Worker process #1:
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
fails
`third good`
is skipped entirely

When running with
retries (https://playwright.dev//Users/sagundevkota/Documents/opensource/autodoc-pre/docs/test-retries/#retries)
, all tests are retried together:

Worker process #1:
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
fails
`third good`
is skipped
Worker process #2:
`beforeAll`
hook runs again
`first good`
passes again
`second flaky`
passes
`third good`
passes

note
It is usually better to make your tests isolated, so they can be efficiently run and retried independently.

## Reuse single page between tests​ {#reuse-single-page-between-tests}

Playwright Test creates an isolated
Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page)
object for each test. However, if you'd like to reuse a single
Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page)
object between multiple tests, you can create your own in
test.beforeAll() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-before-all)
and close it in
test.afterAll() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-after-all)
.

## Execution order​ {#execution-order}

Each fixture has a setup and teardown phase before and after the
`await use()`
call in the fixture. Setup is executed before the test/hook requiring it is run, and teardown is executed when the fixture is no longer being used by the test/hook.

Fixtures follow these rules to determine the execution order:

When fixture A depends on fixture B: B is always set up before A and torn down after A.
Non-automatic fixtures are executed lazily, only when the test/hook needs them.
Test-scoped fixtures are torn down after each test, while worker-scoped fixtures are only torn down when the worker process executing tests is torn down.

Consider the following example:


`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';consttest=base.extend<{testFixture:string,autoTestFixture:string,unusedFixture:string,},{workerFixture:string,autoWorkerFixture:string,}>({workerFixture:[async({browser})=>{// workerFixture setup...awaituse('workerFixture');// workerFixture teardown...},{scope:'worker'}],autoWorkerFixture:[async({browser})=>{// autoWorkerFixture setup...awaituse('autoWorkerFixture');// autoWorkerFixture teardown...},{scope:'worker',auto:true}],testFixture:[async({page,workerFixture})=>{// testFixture setup...awaituse('testFixture');// testFixture teardown...},{scope:'test'}],autoTestFixture:[async()=>{// autoTestFixture setup...awaituse('autoTestFixture');// autoTestFixture teardown...},{scope:'test',auto:true}],unusedFixture:[async({page})=>{// unusedFixture setup...awaituse('unusedFixture');// unusedFixture teardown...},{scope:'test'}],});test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test.beforeEach(async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('first test',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second test',async({testFixture})=>{/* ... */});test.afterEach(async()=>{/* ... */});test.afterAll(async()=>{/* ... */});`

The provided text details various methods available within the `locator` class, primarily focusing on element interaction, data retrieval, and state management:

**Data Retrieval Methods**
*   **`innerHTML`**: Returns the `element.innerHTML`.
*   **`innerText`**: Returns the `element.innerText`. For text assertions, it is recommended to use `expect(locator).toHaveText()` with the `useInnerText` option to reduce flakiness.
*   **`textContent`**: Returns the `node.textContent`. Similar to `innerText`, `expect(locator).toHaveText()` is preferred for assertions.
*   **`inputValue`**: Returns the value of `<input>`, `<textarea>`, or `<select>` elements. For assertions, `expect(locator).toHaveValue()` is preferred.
*   **`toString`**: Returns a human-readable representation of the locator based on its description or selector.

**Interaction and Action Methods**
*   **`selectOption`**: Selects one or more options in a `<select>` element using values, labels, or indices. If the element has a `multiple` attribute, all matching options are selected; otherwise, only the first match is selected.
*   **`uncheck`**: Ensures a radio or checkbox element is unchecked.
*   **`scrollIntoViewIfNeeded`**: Waits for actionability checks and scrolls the element into view unless it is already completely visible (as defined by the `IntersectionObserver` ratio).
*   **Hover and Tap**: Both actions scroll the element into view if needed. Hovering uses `page.mouse` to target the center or a specific position, while tapping uses `page.touchscreen` (which requires the browser context's `hasTouch` option to be true). Both methods throw an error if the element is detached from the DOM or if a specified timeout is reached.

**General Configuration**
Several methods (`innerHTML`, `innerText`, `textContent`, and `scrollIntoViewIfNeeded`) accept an optional `timeout` argument in milliseconds. This defaults to `0` (no timeout) but can be modified via the `actionTimeout` config option, `browserContext.setDefaultTimeout()`, or `page.setDefaultTimeout()`.

user_input: How do I run the same suite across desktop and mobile devices with the right emulation each time?
reference: Define a project per device and spread a device descriptor into its use (e.g. devices['Pixel 5']). Projects let you run the same tests under different configurations, and each project applies its device's emulated parameters.
reference_contexts: By using projects you can run your tests in multiple browsers such as chromium, webkit and firefox as well as branded browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. Playwright can also run on emulated tablet and mobile devices.

Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.
llm_response:
To run a test suite across both desktop and mobile devices with the appropriate emulation, you can configure multiple projects within the `playwright.config.ts` file using the `devices` registry.

In the `projects` array of your configuration, you can define separate entries for each target device. For example, you can create one project for desktop by using `...devices['Desktop Chrome']` and another for mobile by using `...devices['iPhone 13']`. 

Playwright will then simulate the specific browser behavior for each device, including the `userAgent`, `screenSize`, `viewport`, and whether `hasTouch` is enabled. 

If you need to customize the emulation further for specific tests:
*   **Viewport:** You can override the device's default viewport in the config file by defining the `viewport` property after destructuring the device, or within a test file using `test.use({viewport: {width: 1600, height: 1200}})`.
*   **Platform-Specific User Agents:** Pre-configured devices assume a specific platform (e.g., "Desktop Chrome" uses a Windows-specific user agent). To use the user agent of the platform actually running the tests, unset the property by setting `userAgent: undefined`.
*   **Mobile Behavior:** You can explicitly set the `isMobile` property to determine if touch events are enabled and if the meta viewport tag is taken into account.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

With Playwright you can test your app on any browser as well as emulate a real device such as a mobile phone or tablet. Simply configure the devices you would like to emulate and Playwright will simulate the browser behavior such as
`"userAgent"`
,
`"screenSize"`
,
`"viewport"`
and if it
`"hasTouch"`
enabled. You can also emulate the
`"geolocation"`
,
`"locale"`
and
`"timezone"`
for all tests or for a specific test as well as set the
`"permissions"`
to show notifications or change the
`"colorScheme"`
.

## Devices​ {#devices}

Playwright comes with a
registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json)
using
playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices)
for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

The provided text details the API classes for interacting with Android devices in Playwright, primarily focusing on the `androidDevice`, `AndroidInput`, and `AndroidSocket` classes.

### androidDevice Class
This class provides a wide range of methods for device management, information retrieval, and widget interaction.

*   **Device Management & Information:**
    *   **Information:** `info` returns widget information via a selector; `model` provides the device model; `serial` provides the serial number.
    *   **Management:** `installApk` installs an APK (via path or content) with optional `args`; `push` copies a file to the device with an optional `mode` (defaults to 644); `screenshot` captures the device screen as a buffer or saves it to a specified `path`; `close` disconnects from the device.
    *   **Shell Execution:** `shell` executes a command and returns a Buffer, while `open` executes a command and returns an `AndroidSocket`.
    *   **Browser:** `launchBrowser` launches a browser with optional `args` and an `acceptDownloads` setting (defaults to `true`).

*   **Widget Interaction (Added in v1.9):**
    *   **Basic Actions:** `tap` (taps a widget), `fill` (fills an input box with text), `press` (presses a key within a widget), and `longTap` (performs a long tap).
    *   **Gestures:** `drag` (drags a selector to x/y coordinates), `swipe` (swipes a selector in a specified direction by a percentage), `fling` (flings a selector in a direction with optional `speed`), `pinchOpen` and `pinchClose` (pinches a selector based on a percentage and optional `speed`), and `scroll` (scrolls a selector in a direction by a percentage).
    *   **Utility:** `wait` waits for a selector to appear or disappear.

*   **Configuration:**
    *   The `setDefaultTimeout()` method modifies the default value for operations.
    *   Optional `options` for drag, scroll, and swipe include `speed` (pixels per second) and `timeout` (defaults to 30 seconds; `0` disables it).
    *   Using a `null` value for certain configurations opts out of default presets, making the viewport dependent on the host window size, which can lead to non-deterministic test execution.

### AndroidInput Class (Added in v1.9)
This class provides methods that return a `Promise<void>` for direct device interaction:
*   **`tap(point)`**: Taps at specific x/y coordinates.
*   **`type`**: Types a string into the currently focused widget.
*   **`press`**: Presses a specified `AndroidKey`.
*   **`drag`**: Drags from a start point to an end point; each step takes 5 milliseconds.
*   **`swipe`**: Swipes along a path defined by `segments`; each step takes 5 milliseconds.

### AndroidSocket Class
This class manages socket connections to the device:
*   **Methods:** `write` sends Buffer data to the socket, and `close` closes the connection.
*   **Events:** Emits `on('data')` when data is available as a Buffer and `on('close')` when the socket is closed.

### Additional Features
*   **HAR Recording:** Supports a `path` and a `mode` (`full` or `minimal`). Resources can be `attach`ed (default for `.zip`) or `embed`ded.
*   **Video Recording:** `recordVideo` options allow specifying a directory (`dir`) and frame `width`.

    *   `screen`: Emulates `window.screen` size (width and height) and is only used when a viewport is set.

*   `javaScriptEnabled`: Controls whether JavaScript is enabled (defaults to `true`).

*   Videos are recorded into the `recordVideo.dir` directory if specified.
*   `height`: Sets the video frame height. If not specified, it scales the viewport to fit 800x800, or defaults to 800x450 if no viewport is configured.

### **Core Classes and Methods**
*   **Android Class**: Used for initial connection and server management.
    *   `connect`: Attaches to a device via a browser websocket endpoint.
    *   `launchServer`: Starts a Playwright Android server. Options include `adbHost` (default `127.0.0.1`), `adbPort` (default `5037`), `deviceSerialNumber`, `host`, `port`, `wsPath` (recommended to use a custom token for security), and `omitDriverInstall`.
    *   `devices`: Returns a list of detected devices.
    *   `setDefaultTimeout`: Sets the default maximum time for operations.
*   **AndroidDevice Class**: Manages a specific device.
    *   **Properties/Methods**: `model()` and `serial` return device identification; `shell` executes shell commands; `open()` launches a shell process.
    *   **WebView Management**: `webView(selector, options)` returns or creates a WebView (with optional `pkg` and `socketName`), and `webViews()` lists all open WebViews.
    *   **Interactions**: Includes `wait(selector, options)` (to wait for an element to be present or 'gone'), `waitForEvent(event, optionsOrPredicate)`, and an `input` property of type `AndroidInput`.
    *   **Events**: Emits `close` when the connection ends and `webview` when a new WebView is detected.
*   **AndroidWebView Class**:
    *   `page()`: Returns a Playwright `Page` for interaction.
    *   `pid()` and `pkg()`: Return the process PID and package identifier.
    *   **Events**: Emits `close` when the WebView is closed.

### **Browser Launch and Emulation Options**
When launching a browser on an Android device, several configuration options are available:
*   **Emulation**: 
    *   **Media**: `colorScheme` ('light'/'dark'), `contrast` ('no-preference'/'more'), `forcedColors` ('none'/'active'), and `reducedMotion` ('no-preference'/'reduce'). Passing `null` resets these to system defaults.
    *   **Viewport/Device**: `deviceScaleFactor` (default `1`), `viewport` (default 1280x720; `null` makes it dependent on host window size), `screen` (used if viewport is set), `isMobile` (enables touch events and meta viewport tag), and `hasTouch`.
*   **Behavior**: `javaScriptEnabled` (default `true`), `serviceWorkers` ('allow'/'block'), `strictSelectors` (boolean), `accuracy` (default `0`), `offline` (boolean), and `permissions` (list of granted permissions).
*   **Network**: `extraHTTPHeaders` can be provided for all requests.

### **Video Recording and Timeouts**
*   **Video Recording**: Videos are saved to `recordVideo.dir`. Options include `height` (defaults to 800x450 or scales to 800x800), and `showActions` (visual annotations with configurable `duration`, `position`, and `fontSize`).
*   **Timeouts and Timing**: 
    *   Most operations default to a `timeout` of 30,000ms (30 seconds), which can be disabled by passing `0` or modified via `setDefaultTimeout()`.
    *   `slowMo` can be used to slow down operations by a specified number of milliseconds.
    *   `duration` is specifically used to define the length of a tap in milliseconds.

user_input: I want the same fixture to behave differently per project — say a default item that changes. How do option fixtures and projects combine?
reference: Declare an 'option' fixture with a default value, then override that value per project in the config's use block. The fixture reads the option, so each project drives its own behavior in a type-safe way.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test supports running multiple test projects that can be configured separately. You can use "option" fixtures to make your configuration options declarative and type safe. Learn more about parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize) .
You can also use projects to run the same tests in different configurations. For example, you can run the same tests in a logged-in and logged-out state.
llm_response:
To make a fixture behave differently per project, you can define it as an option fixture by specifying `option: true` when defining the fixture. This allows the fixture to receive a value specified in the configuration file or fall back to a default value.

In the configuration file, you can then set different values for this option within the `use` object of each project. For example, if you have a `defaultItem` option, you can define one project (e.g., 'shopping') with `defaultItem: 'Buy milk'` and another project (e.g., 'wellbeing') with `defaultItem: 'Exercise!'`. The fixture will then use the value corresponding to the project currently being executed.
llm_references:
my-test.ts

`import{testasbase}from'@playwright/test';import{TodoPage}from'./todo-page';// Declare your options to type-check your configuration.exporttypeMyOptions={defaultItem:string;};typeMyFixtures={todoPage:TodoPage;};// Specify both option and fixture types.exportconsttest=base.extend<MyOptions&MyFixtures>({// Define an option and provide a default value.// We can later override it in the config.defaultItem:['Something nice',{option:true}],// Our "todoPage" fixture depends on the option.todoPage:async({page,defaultItem},use)=>{consttodoPage=newTodoPage(page);awaittodoPage.goto();awaittodoPage.addToDo(defaultItem);awaituse(todoPage);awaittodoPage.removeAll();},});export{expect}from'@playwright/test';`


We can now use the
`todoPage`
fixture as usual, and set the
`defaultItem`
option in the configuration file.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';importtype{MyOptions}from'./my-test';exportdefaultdefineConfig<MyOptions>({projects:[{name:'shopping',use:{defaultItem:'Buy milk'},},{name:'wellbeing',use:{defaultItem:'Exercise!'},},]});`


Array as an option value

If the value of your option is an array, for example
`[{ name: 'Alice' }, { name: 'Bob' }]`
, you'll need to wrap it into an extra array when providing the value. This is best illustrated with an example.


`typePerson={name:string};consttest=base.extend<{persons:Person[]}>({// Declare the option, default value is an empty array.persons:[[],{option:true}],});// Option value is an array of persons.constactualPersons=[{name:'Alice'},{name:'Bob'}];test.use({// CORRECT: Wrap the value into an array and pass the scope.persons:[actualPersons,{scope:'test'}],});test.use({// WRONG: passing an array value directly will not work.persons:actualPersons,});`
